courseDescription: A comprehensive technical journey from the probabilistic foundations of language modeling to the deployment of production-grade LLM applications. This course covers the internal mechanics of Transformers, the nuances of pretraining and alignment, and advanced orchestration patterns including Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) and autonomous agents.
targetLearner: Aspiring AI engineers and data scientists who want to move beyond simple API calls to understand how modern generative models are built, fine-tuned, and deployed in high-stakes environments.

projects.project_name: Building a Research Synthesis Agent: From Embeddings to Production
projects.project_description: In this project, you will build a sophisticated LLM-powered research assistant. You will start by implementing foundational tokenization and vector search, move to configuring a fine-tuned model using LoRA, build a complete Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) system with agentic tool-use capabilities, and finally implement a rigorous evaluation and safety suite to ensure production readiness.
projects.final_deliverable: A production-grade Python application featuring a RAG-based Research Agent with custom tool-calling, a LoRA-adapted model backbone, and an automated evaluation report quantifying hallucination rates and retrieval accuracy.

units.title: From Language Models to Generation
units.description: Establish the foundational bridge between linguistic probability and modern generative models by exploring tokenization, vector semantics, and the generative landscape.

lectures.title: What a Language Model Is
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the probabilistic heart of LLMs, moving from the conceptual definition of modeling language to the practical mechanics of how models handle raw text.

sessions.title: Language as Probability
sessions.description: This session introduces the mathematical view of language as a statistical distribution where sequences of words are assigned likelihoods. You will learn to think of a model not as a database of facts, but as a predictive engine estimating $P(w_n | w_1, ..., w_{n-1})$. This foundational shift is essential for mastering how generative AI navigates uncertainty and creates fluent text.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common misconception that Large Language Models (LLMs) are vast databases or 'libraries' of stored facts. On the whiteboard, draw a large brain icon crossed out next to a calculator icon. Explain that we must shift our mental model from 'retrieval' to 'prediction.' The core objective here is to establish that every word an AI generates is the result of a mathematical gamble based on patterns, not a search for truth. This distinction is vital because it explains why models can sound incredibly confident while being factually wrong—they are maximizing probability, not verifying reality.

Introduce the concept of 'Language as a Distribution' by writing a simple sentence fragment on the board: 'The cat sat on the...'. Ask the students to shout out what comes next. As they say 'mat,' 'floor,' or 'hat,' write these words down with associated percentages (e.g., mat: 60%, floor: 20%, etc.). Use this to define the fundamental formula $P(w_n | w_1, ..., w_{n-1})$. Explain that the model’s entire existence is dedicated to filling in that 'n-th' word based on everything that came before it. The 'intuition' here is that language has structure, and because it has structure, it is statistically predictable.

Transition into why high probability usually equates to 'human-like' coherence. Explain that in any language, certain sequences are statistically 'favored' because they follow grammatical rules and logical physical constraints (e.g., 'drinking water' is more probable than 'drinking rocks'). Draw a branching tree diagram starting from a single word to show how small choices at each step lead to vastly different narratives. This helps learners see that the 'fluency' they admire in ChatGPT is actually the model successfully navigating a high-dimensional map of word associations it learned during training.

Address the 'Uncertainty' factor by introducing a scenario where the prefix is ambiguous, such as 'He went to the...'. Point out that the probability distribution here is much 'flatter'—there are many valid completions like 'bank,' 'store,' or 'park.' Use this to explain that the model doesn't just pick one; it calculates a weight for all of them. This sets the stage for future discussions on 'temperature' and 'sampling.' A common pitfall for beginners is thinking the model 'knows' the right answer; emphasize that the model only knows the most 'likely' answer based on its training data.

Conclude with a brief interactive exercise where students must calculate simple conditional probabilities based on a tiny 'toy' dataset you provide on the board (e.g., three sentences total). By manually counting occurrences to find the likelihood of the next word, they demystify the 'AI' label and replace it with 'statistical inference.' This hands-on moment is designed to prove that the 'magic' of LLMs is actually just math performed at a massive scale, providing the necessary grounding for when we move into more complex architectures like Transformers.

tasks: Calculate simple conditional probabilities for short word sequences.
Explain why high-probability sequences often result in coherent human language.

sessions.title: Next-Token Prediction
sessions.description: This session explores the iterative process where a model generates content by repeatedly choosing the most likely next unit of text. You will learn how autoregressive generation works and why the model's own previous outputs become its future inputs. Understanding this loop is critical for diagnosing generation errors and understanding why context windows matter.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by positioning the concept of 'Autoregressive Generation' as the engine of modern AI. Since the learner has indicated no specific technical preference, avoid starting with heavy notation. Instead, visualize a whiteboard with a simple, incomplete sentence: 'The best thing about coding is...'. Explain that the model does not see the whole answer at once; it only sees what has come before. This is the moment to introduce the 'loop'—the core idea that the output of step N becomes the mandatory input for step N+1. This framing is vital because it demystifies how a static statistical model can produce dynamic, long-form creative writing.

Draw a flowchart on the board representing the cycle: Input -> Inference -> Distribution -> Selection -> Update Context. Use the word 'The' as the initial input. Show the model generating a probability distribution for the next token (e.g., 'cat' 1%, 'weather' 2%, 'future' 15%). The most important pedagogical point here is that the model's 'knowledge' is frozen, but its 'state' is constantly evolving as it adds its own choices back into its context window. This explains why errors early in a sentence often lead to a 'hallucination spiral'—if the model chooses a low-probability word by mistake, it must then justify that word in all subsequent steps.

Transition to the mechanic of 'Selection' by contrasting 'Greedy Search' with 'Sampling.' On the whiteboard, show a scenario where the top three tokens are nearly equal in probability. Explain that if we always pick the most likely word (Greedy), the AI becomes repetitive and boring, like a person who only speaks in cliches. Then, introduce the concept of 'Temperature' as a dial that flattens or sharpens this probability hill. This allows the teacher to address a common misconception: that LLMs are 'searching' for a right answer. In reality, they are rolling dice on a weighted table. Use a specific exercise here: ask the learner to predict what happens to the sentence 'Once upon a...' if the temperature is set to zero versus a very high value. This reveals whether they grasp the trade-off between coherence and creativity.

Conclude by discussing the 'Context Window' constraint through the lens of this loop. Visualize the input sequence getting longer and longer until it hits a physical limit. Explain that once a token falls out of the 'back' of the window, the model effectively 'forgets' it, even if it wrote that token itself five minutes ago. This architectural reality explains why long conversations eventually lose the thread. The teacher should emphasize that the 'Next-Token Prediction' loop is both the model's greatest strength—allowing for infinite flexibility—and its fundamental limitation, as it lacks a global 'plan' for the text it is creating.

tasks: Trace an autoregressive generation loop for a three-word sentence.
Identify the difference between greedy choice and probabilistic sampling.

sessions.title: Tokenization
sessions.description: This session dives into the bridge between human text and machine numbers through Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) and other subword methods. You will learn why models see 'apple' differently than 'apples' and how the choice of tokenizer impacts the model's vocabulary. This technical knowledge is vital for understanding common LLM failures in spelling, math, and non-English languages.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by challenging the intuitive assumption that computers 'read' text. We must break the illusion that a Large Language Model sees the word 'intelligence' as a single semantic unit. On the whiteboard, draw a clear line between 'Human World (Characters)' and 'Machine World (Numbers)'. Explain that while previous sessions focused on the probability of the next 'unit,' this session defines what that unit actually is. Introduce the 'Token' as the fundamental atom of LLM cognition. The most critical takeaway here is that LLMs do not process characters or words, but statistical chunks, which explains why they often struggle with tasks that seem trivial to humans, like counting letters in a word or reversing a string.

Transition into the mechanics of Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) by illustrating the 'Character-Word Gap.' If we use characters, our sequences are too long and computationally expensive; if we use whole words, our vocabulary becomes infinite and cannot handle typos or new terms. Use the whiteboard to demonstrate a simplified BPE merge process. Start with a small corpus like 'low', 'lower', 'newest', and 'widest'. Show the iterative process of counting the most frequent pairs (e.g., 'e' and 's') and merging them into a new token ('es'). This visualization helps learners realize that tokenization is an optimization problem—trying to represent the most information with the fewest tokens.

Address the 'Apple vs. Apples' problem to highlight how tokenization affects semantic relationships. On the whiteboard, show how a tokenizer might split 'apple' as one token but 'apples' as [apple, s]. Explain that to the model, the connection between a singular and plural noun is not inherent but learned through the coincidence of these tokens appearing together. This is where you address the misconception that models 'understand' grammar; they actually navigate a numerical space defined by how these subword fragments cluster. Warn the students that if a tokenizer is inefficient—splitting a common word into many meaningless fragments—the model's 'intelligence' on that topic will drop significantly because it has to spend more of its context window just to 'see' the word.

Introduce a brief 'manual trace' exercise: give the learners a short string like 'abacaba' and ask them to perform two rounds of BPE merges. The goal is to reveal how the 'vocabulary' grows while the 'sequence length' shrinks. While they work, walk around and look for the common mistake of merging pairs that aren't adjacent or failing to update the frequency count after a merge. Use these mistakes to explain why pre-training a tokenizer on a representative dataset is just as important as training the model itself; if the tokenizer hasn't 'seen' enough code or non-English text, it will over-fragment those inputs, making them more expensive and harder for the model to process.

Conclude by connecting tokenization to 'LLM weirdness'—specifically failures in spelling, math, and cross-language performance. Explain that when a model fails to spell a word correctly, it is often because that word is a single token; the model never 'saw' the individual letters. Use the example of large numbers (e.g., 123456) being split differently (e.g., [12, 34, 56] vs [123, 456]) depending on the tokenizer. This explains why LLMs can be inconsistent with arithmetic. End by emphasizing that as developers, they must always inspect how their specific model 'sees' their prompt, as the 'token tax' determines both the financial cost and the cognitive limit of the system.

tasks: Manually perform a basic BPE merge on a provided text string.
Compare how different tokenizers split complex technical terms.

sessions.title: Vocabulary, Context, and Cost
sessions.description: This session connects the technical constraints of vocabulary size and context window length to the economic reality of token-based pricing. You will learn how to estimate the memory and cost requirements of a prompt and why 'more tokens' isn't always better for model performance. This provides the pragmatic framework needed to build cost-effective AI applications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by bridging the gap between the abstract math of tokenization and the hard reality of engineering constraints. The whiteboard should initially feature three distinct columns: 'The Dictionary' (Vocabulary), 'The Stage' (Context Window), and 'The Bill' (Cost). This session aims to show that every design choice in an LLM involves a trade-off. We start by explaining that the 'Vocabulary' isn't just a list; it is a fixed-size embedding matrix. A larger vocabulary (e.g., 100k tokens vs 50k) allows the model to represent complex concepts or non-English scripts more efficiently, but at the cost of significantly higher memory overhead. This is the first 'aha' moment: more words in the dictionary make the model 'smarter' at reading, but 'heavier' to store.

Moving to the 'Context Window,' we visualize this as a sliding frame over a sequence. Use a diagram of a conveyor belt to illustrate that once the window is full, the earliest information must be 'forgotten' to make room for new tokens. It is crucial to address the misconception that context windows are infinite; explain that because of the quadratic nature of standard attention (which we will touch on in later units), doubling the context window doesn't just double the work—it quadruples the computational 'weight.' This explains why long-form document analysis is fundamentally more difficult than short chat interactions.

Now, we connect these technical limits to 'The Bill.' In the API economy, users are billed for what they send (prompt) and what the model returns (completion). I will draw a scenario on the board: a developer builds a RAG system that feeds a 50-page PDF into a prompt. We calculate the math together—if a page is roughly 800 tokens, a 50-page prompt is 40,000 tokens. At current market rates, a single query could cost several cents. This calculation exercise is vital because it reveals the 'hidden tax' of inefficient tokenization. If a tokenizer is poor and splits a single word into five tokens, the developer is essentially paying a 500% markup for the same semantic meaning.

To wrap up, we transition into a practice moment where students evaluate the 'Efficiency Frontier.' We present two models: Model A with a massive 128k context window but high latency, and Model B with an 8k window but lightning-fast response times. The goal of this exercise is to force students to realize that 'bigger' isn't always 'better.' The most important takeaway is that an LLM engineer's job is to optimize the 'Information Density'—getting the most reasoning out of the fewest possible tokens. This sets the stage for future discussions on prompt engineering and RAG, where token management becomes a primary survival skill.

tasks: Calculate the token count and estimated API cost for a sample dataset.
Evaluate the trade-offs between a large vocabulary and model latency.

lectures.title: Representing Meaning
lectures.description: This lecture explains the geometric representation of language, showing how models use high-dimensional space to understand relationship, nuance, and intent.

sessions.title: Word Embeddings
sessions.description: This session introduces the transition from discrete words to continuous vectors, often called 'embeddings.' You will learn how words are mapped into a high-dimensional space where spatial proximity reflects semantic similarity. This is the first step in understanding how AI 'understands' the relationships between concepts like 'king' and 'queen'.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by acknowledging the fundamental friction between human language and machine computation: computers are exceptional at processing numbers but historically poor at understanding the 'fuzziness' of words. The teacher should start the whiteboard by writing the word 'Apple' and asking the audience what it means. Is it a fruit? A tech company? A symbol of temptation? To a computer, the word 'Apple' is just an arbitrary string of characters or a unique integer ID (a token). The core problem we are solving today is how to transform these discrete, cold labels into a mathematical format that actually captures their essence. This is where we introduce the concept of 'Embeddings'—the bridge between the symbolic world of human speech and the geometric world of high-dimensional math.

To visualize this, the teacher draws a simple Cartesian plane (2D) on the whiteboard. Place 'King' at a specific coordinate and 'Queen' nearby. Explain that in a computer's 'mind,' words aren't just names; they are locations. If 'King' is at (5, 5), 'Queen' might be at (5, 6). The proximity matters. The most important takeaway here is that distance equals meaning. If two words are close in this space, they are semantically related. This shifts the learner's perspective from seeing AI as a dictionary-lookup tool to seeing it as a spatial navigator. We must warn students here that while we draw in 2D for clarity, real models operate in 768 or 1536 dimensions—a 'hyper-space' we cannot see but can calculate.

Next, the teacher should demonstrate the 'Vector Math of Meaning.' On the whiteboard, draw a vector from 'Man' to 'Woman.' Then, draw a parallel vector starting from 'King.' Where does it land? Ideally, it lands on 'Queen.' The teacher should explain the logic: [King] - [Man] + [Woman] = [Queen]. This isn't just a party trick; it proves that the model has 'learned' the concept of gender as a specific direction in space. This is a critical moment for the student: they realize that intelligence in LLMs emerges from these geometric relationships. The teacher should pause here to address a common misconception: models don't 'know' what a King is in the human sense; they only know that 'King' relates to 'Man' the same way 'Queen' relates to 'Woman.'

Transitioning to the first practice task, the teacher prompts the students to imagine a 2D projection of a massive dataset. Ask them: 'If we have words like 'Car', 'Truck', 'Apple', and 'Banana', how would they cluster?' This exercise is designed to reveal if they understand the concept of 'semantic clusters.' A student might mistakenly think 'Car' and 'Apple' could be close because they are both 'objects.' The teacher must correct this by emphasizing that the model groups things based on usage context—'Car' and 'Truck' belong to the transportation cluster, while 'Apple' and 'Banana' belong to the fruit cluster.

Finally, the teacher wraps up by discussing the 'Magnitude' and 'Direction' of these vectors. Use the whiteboard to show that a vector isn't just a point, but an arrow from the origin. This sets the stage for the next session on Similarity. Explain that even if our human brains cannot visualize a 1000-dimension vector, the math of measuring the angle between these arrows stays the same. This session ends by leaving the learner with the realization that every word they type into an LLM is immediately converted into a long list of numbers—a 'coordinate' in the vast map of human knowledge.

tasks: Visualize 2D projections of high-dimensional word vectors.
Perform vector addition/subtraction to find semantic analogies (e.g., King - Man + Woman).

sessions.title: Vector Semantics and Similarity
sessions.description: This session focuses on the mathematical tools used to measure meaning, specifically Cosine Similarity and Euclidean distance. You will learn how to quantify how 'close' two pieces of text are in a model's latent space. Mastering these metrics is the prerequisite for building search and retrieval systems in later units.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by bridging from the previous discussion on embeddings. While the previous session established that words live in a high-dimensional space, this session answers the critical engineering question: how do we actually measure the distance between two thoughts? Begin the whiteboard visualization by drawing a simple 2D coordinate system with two vectors representing 'cat' and 'dog' pointing in a similar direction, and a third vector for 'skyscraper' pointing far away. This visual sets the stage for defining 'Meaning' as a spatial relationship, emphasizing that in AI, similarity is not a binary 'yes/no' but a scalar value between -1 and 1.

Introduce Euclidean Distance first because it is the most intuitive for students familiar with high-school geometry. On the whiteboard, draw the straight-line 'as-the-crow-flies' path between the tips of the two vectors. Explain the Pythagorean logic here: it measures the literal gap between points. However, immediately introduce the 'Magnitude Trap.' Illustrate a scenario where a short sentence and a long paragraph discuss the same topic. Their directions are the same, but the long paragraph's vector is much 'longer' (greater magnitude) because it contains more word occurrences. This creates a large Euclidean distance despite high semantic similarity. This realization is the 'Aha!' moment that justifies why we need a different metric for language.

Transition to Cosine Similarity by focusing on the angle between vectors rather than the distance between their tips. Draw two vectors of vastly different lengths but the same orientation. Show that the angle theta (θ) is zero, meaning they are perfectly aligned. Write the formula on the board, but focus on the intuition: the dot product normalized by the magnitudes. Explain that in high-dimensional AI spaces, the 'direction' represents the concept (the 'what'), while the 'length' often represents the frequency or confidence (the 'how much'). By focusing on the cosine of the angle, we isolate the meaning from the length of the text, which is why it is the industry standard for search and RAG systems.

Engage the students in a conceptual calculation task. Ask them to imagine three vectors: V1 (Apple the fruit), V2 (Pear), and V3 (Apple the tech company). Use this to demonstrate that V1 and V2 might have a high cosine similarity because they share 'fruit' context, while V1 and V3—despite sharing the same word—will point in different directions in a well-trained latent space. This exercise helps students realize that similarity metrics are only as good as the underlying embeddings. If the model hasn't disambiguated the context yet, the math will reflect that failure.

Conclude by addressing a common misconception: that high similarity always means 'synonym.' Clarify that 'hot' and 'cold' often have very high cosine similarity because they appear in identical contexts (e.g., 'The weather is ___'). Explain that similarity metrics measure 'relatedness' or 'contextual sharedness' rather than just agreement. This distinction is vital for future units where students will build retrieval systems, as they need to understand that the model retrieves things that are *relevant* to the query's space, not necessarily the exact answer.

tasks: Compute the cosine similarity between three sample vectors.
Explain why cosine similarity is often preferred over Euclidean distance for text.

sessions.title: Contextual Representations
sessions.description: This session explains why modern LLMs use dynamic embeddings rather than static ones, allowing the word 'bank' to have different vectors in 'river bank' vs 'investment bank.' You will learn how models look at surrounding tokens to update meaning. This transitions your understanding from simple lookup tables to the sophisticated contextual engines of today.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by drawing a large, static dot on the whiteboard labeled 'Bank'. Remind the students of the previous session where we treated words as fixed coordinates in space. Now, write two sentences around that dot: 'The fisherman sat on the river bank' and 'The investor walked into the bank.' Ask the students to consider if a single coordinate can truly capture the essence of both sentences. The core realization here is that in human language, meaning is not a property of the word alone, but a property of its relationship with its neighbors. This is the fundamental limitation of static embeddings like Word2Vec—they are 'deaf' to the context, providing a 'blurry average' of all possible meanings.

Transition the visualization by drawing arrows from 'fisherman' and 'river' pointing toward the 'Bank' dot. Explain that in a contextual model, these neighboring words pull the original vector toward a specific region of the semantic space—perhaps a 'nature/geography' zone. Conversely, 'investor' and 'money' pull it toward a 'finance' zone. The most important concept to convey is that a modern LLM doesn't just look up a vector; it 'computes' a vector on the fly based on the surrounding tokens. This allows the model to handle polysemy (words with multiple meanings) and nuance that static systems simply cannot reach.

Introduce the 'Interaction Layer' concept. On the whiteboard, draw the input tokens as a row of dots and show how every token 'talks' to every other token. Explain that this dialogue is what allows the model to resolve ambiguity. A common misconception for students is thinking that the model just picks one definition from a dictionary; clarify instead that the model is performing a weighted transformation of the vector. The 'Bank' vector literally shifts its coordinates in the high-dimensional space as it 'notices' the word 'river' nearby. This is why we call them 'dynamic' embeddings.

To solidify this, engage the students in an identification exercise. Ask them to brainstorm other 'chameleon words' like 'cell' (biology vs. prison vs. phone) or 'apple' (fruit vs. tech company). Ask them to describe what specific neighboring words would act as the 'gravitational pull' for each meaning. This exercise reveals whether students understand that context isn't just 'extra information,' but the primary architect of the final representation. 

Conclude by contrasting the architecture of a lookup table (static) with the architecture of a Transformer (contextual). Explain that while static embeddings are like a printed dictionary, contextual representations are like a live conversation where the meaning of a word is constantly being negotiated. This sets the stage for the next session on sequence length, as the more context a model can 'see' simultaneously, the more precise these dynamic representations become. Explain that this shift from static to dynamic is what truly unlocked the 'intelligence' we see in GPT-style models.

tasks: Identify polysemous words and describe how their context changes their meaning.
Differentiate between Word2Vec (static) and Transformer (contextual) approaches.

sessions.title: Sequence Length and Memory
sessions.description: This session addresses the technical bottleneck of long sequences and the quadratic scaling of traditional attention. You will learn why models have a 'context limit' and the implications of that limit for processing large documents. This sets the stage for understanding the architectural innovations you will see in Unit 2.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by bridging the gap between the geometric beauty of embeddings and the harsh reality of hardware limitations. I want to start by drawing a simple line representing a sequence of tokens—let’s say, a sentence. Underneath it, draw a grid. This grid represents the 'Attention Matrix' where every word looks at every other word. The core message here is the 'Quadratic Tax': if you double the number of words, you don't just double the work; you quadruple it. This concept is vital because it explains why LLMs aren't infinite libraries and why 'memory' in AI is fundamentally different from a hard drive. It justifies the existence of 'Context Windows' not as a design choice, but as a physical constraint of VRAM.

To make this concrete, visualize the math without getting lost in the weeds. Draw a 2x2 grid representing 2 tokens, then an 8x8 grid representing 8 tokens. Explain that for a model to 'understand' context, every token must hold a score for its relationship with every other token. This is the 'N-squared' problem. The most important takeaway is that as we scale from a 2,000-token prompt to an 8,000-token prompt, the memory required for these attention scores increases by 16 times, not 4. I often see learners assume that more data just takes a bit more time; we must correct this by emphasizing that this quadratic growth eventually hits a 'memory wall' where the GPU simply runs out of room to hold the relationship map.

Next, introduce the concept of 'Context Truncation' using a physical metaphor. Imagine a conveyor belt that can only hold 50 feet of items; as a new item comes on the front, the oldest item must fall off the back. This is how many LLMs handle long conversations. The danger here is 'Loss of Coherence.' If the model's window is too small, it will 'forget' the beginning of the prompt even if the text is still technically in the chat history. We should pose a thought experiment to the learners: if you ask a model to summarize a 50-page legal document but its window is only 10 pages, what happens to the middle? This reveals the invisible 'blind spots' in AI reasoning that students must be aware of when designing real-world applications.

Finally, lead into a whiteboard estimation exercise. We will walk through a back-of-the-envelope calculation comparing a 2k context vs an 8k context. Instead of just giving the answer, ask the students to visualize the 'Attention Matrix' area. This exercise is designed to reveal if they truly grasp the scale of quadratic growth. We conclude by hinting at the innovations in Unit 2, such as 'Sparse Attention' or 'Flash Attention,' which act as the engineering 'tricks' used to cheat this quadratic math. This session leaves them with a healthy respect for the token limit and prepares them for the architectural deep dives to follow.

tasks: Estimate the memory usage for a model with a 2k context vs an 8k context.
Discuss the impact of context truncation on model coherence.

lectures.title: The Generative Landscape
lectures.description: This lecture provides a high-level overview of the capabilities and boundaries of current generative AI, spanning different modalities and use cases.

sessions.title: Text Generation
sessions.description: This session categorizes the types of text-based tasks LLMs excel at, from summarization to creative writing and code generation. You will learn how different model flavors are optimized for specific outcomes. This allows you to select the right tool for different application development goals.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a simple dividing line on the whiteboard to distinguish between 'The Predictor' and 'The Assistant.' Since the learner is approaching this from a concept-first public lecture style, we must move beyond the mystery of the chat box. Explain that text generation is not a monolithic capability; it is the byproduct of different training stages. On the left side of the board, write 'Base Model' and describe it as a hyper-competent student who has read the entire internet but doesn't know how to follow directions. Use an example like asking a base model 'What is the capital of France?' and explain why it might respond with 'What is the capital of Germany?'—it is simply completing a pattern of quiz questions rather than answering one. This distinction is vital because it helps the learner understand that 'intelligence' in LLMs is often a mix of raw knowledge and specifically tuned behavior.

Transition to the right side of the board under the label 'Instruction-Tuned.' Here, explain how the model is refined to understand the intent behind a prompt. This is the first major pedagogical beat: the shift from 'Next Token Prediction' to 'Instruction Following.' Visualize this by drawing a funnel. Raw data goes in the top, but 'Alignment' (SFT/RLHF) shapes the output to be helpful, honest, and harmless. For our concept-first learner, emphasize that when we talk about 'Generative AI,' we are usually interacting with this tuned layer. This explains why certain models feel 'personable' while others feel like raw engines. If the learner mistakenly thinks models 'know' things like humans do, this is the moment to ground them in the reality that it is still just probability, just more focused probability.

Now, categorize the tasks that define the modern text-generation landscape. Group them into three clusters: Transformation, Expansion, and Logic. For 'Transformation,' focus on summarization and style transfer—taking existing information and changing its shape. For 'Expansion,' focus on creative writing and brainstorming—where the model provides high variance. For 'Logic,' focus on code generation and step-by-step reasoning. On the whiteboard, map these tasks on a spectrum of 'Creativity' vs. 'Constraint.' Explain that a task like 'writing a poem' thrives on the model's stochastic nature, while 'writing Python code' requires the model to be heavily constrained by syntax and logic. This prevents the common misconception that an LLM is equally good at all tasks; the teacher should highlight that the 'hallucination' which ruins a legal brief is the exact same 'imagination' that makes a science fiction story compelling.

Conclude by introducing the concept of 'Model Flavors' or specialized architectures. Mention that while a general-purpose GPT-4 is a jack-of-all-trades, there are models specifically distilled for coding (like CodeLlama) or medical advice. The logic here is to show that application development isn't just about the biggest model, but the right model for the specific constraints of the task. Use the practice moment of comparing base vs. instruction-tuned outputs to prove this point. By asking the learner to identify which tasks require high reasoning versus high creativity, you are forcing them to evaluate the 'stochastic' vs 'deterministic' needs of a project, which is the foundational skill for any AI engineer or architect.

tasks: Compare outputs from an instruction-tuned model vs a base model for the same prompt.
List three text generation tasks that require high reasoning vs high creativity.

sessions.title: Image and Audio Generation
sessions.description: This session briefly introduces non-text modalities, explaining the conceptual similarities between predicting the next token and predicting pixels or audio waveforms. You will learn how Diffusion and GANs differ from LLMs. This broadens your perspective of Generative AI beyond just chat interfaces.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a simple line on the board representing a sequence of time. Remind the learners that in Unit 1, we defined Language Models as 'next-token predictors'—a linear, one-way street from left to right. Now, bridge this to the visual and auditory world. Explain that while text feels discrete (words are distinct units), images and audio feel continuous. The core conceptual leap here is that generative AI treats almost everything as a 'density estimation' problem: whether we are predicting the next word, the next pixel, or the next millisecond of sound, the model is trying to guess the most likely value based on what it has seen before.

Introduce the concept of Diffusion as a 'sculpting' process to contrast with the LLM's 'writing' process. On the whiteboard, draw a cloud of random static (noise). Explain that while an LLM builds a sentence brick-by-brick (autoregressive), a Diffusion model starts with a bucket of messy static and gradually 'denoises' it. Describe the forward process—adding noise to an image until it’s unrecognizable—and then the backward process, where the AI learns to reverse that damage. This is a vital distinction because it shifts the learner's mental model from 'linear prediction' to 'iterative refinement.' Use the analogy of a sculptor starting with a block of marble (the noise) and slowly chipping away at it until a statue emerges, rather than a writer typing one character at a time.

Move to the technical landscape of GANs (Generative Adversarial Networks) vs. Diffusion to address potential confusion between different image generation architectures. Sketch a simple 'Counterfeiter' and 'Police Officer' diagram. The Counterfeiter (Generator) tries to create a fake image, and the Police Officer (Discriminator) tries to spot it. Explain that while GANs are fast, they are notoriously difficult to train because the two 'players' must stay perfectly balanced. Contrast this with the stability of Diffusion, which has become the industry standard because it doesn't require this competitive balancing act. This explains 'why' the industry shifted from the GAN-heavy era of 2018 to the Stable Diffusion/Midjourney era of today.

Transition to audio generation by visualizing sound as a waveform on the board. Show how audio can be treated like text by 'tokenizing' small slices of the waveform or like an image by converting it into a spectrogram (a visual map of frequencies). This is a 'lightbulb moment' for many: if we can turn sound into a picture (spectrogram), we can use image-generation techniques to create music. Point out that the math underneath isn't changing—only the way we represent the data. This demystifies the idea that 'Voice AI' is some entirely different branch of science; it’s often just the same probability engines we’ve been discussing, wearing a different coat.

Conclude by challenging the learners to think about 'high-dimensional' data. Ask them to imagine a use case where multimodal generation—creating an image and a description simultaneously—solves a problem that a simple chatbot cannot, such as medical imaging diagnostics or automated video editing. The goal of this discussion is to prevent the common misconception that LLMs are the 'only' type of generative AI. By the end of this session, the learner should see AI not as a text box, but as a universal translator of probability that can manifest as pixels, phonemes, or paragraphs.

tasks: Contrast the iterative refinement of diffusion models with the sequential generation of LLMs.
Identify a use case where multimodal generation is superior to text-only.

sessions.title: Multimodal Models
sessions.description: This session explains how models are trained to 'see' and 'hear' simultaneously by aligning different embedding spaces (e.g., CLIP). You will learn how a single model can reason about an image and describe it in text. This represents the cutting edge of AI development and prepares you for future agentic workflows.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a fundamental limitation of the LLMs we have discussed so far: they are 'sensory deprived,' living only in a world of text. To bridge this gap, I will start the whiteboard by drawing two separate islands—one representing 'The World of Images' and the other 'The World of Language.' On the image island, data exists as pixel grids; on the language island, it exists as discrete tokens. The core challenge of Multimodal AI is not just building a bridge between these islands, but ensuring that a concept like 'golden retriever' occupies the same mathematical coordinate regardless of whether it is expressed as a JPG file or a string of text.

I will then introduce the concept of the 'Joint Embedding Space' using the CLIP (Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training) architecture as our primary mental model. On the whiteboard, I’ll visualize this as a high-dimensional coordinate system. The key pedagogical move here is to explain 'Alignment.' I will describe the training process: we feed the model a photo of a cat and the text 'a cat sitting on a mat.' Through contrastive learning, the model is penalized if the vector for the image and the vector for the text are far apart, and rewarded when they are pulled together. This is the 'Aha!' moment for students—understanding that the model doesn't 'see' the cat; it maps the visual features into the same neighborhood where the word 'cat' already lives.

Next, we will transition into the mechanics of Vision-Language Models (VLMs) like GPT-4o or LLaVA. I will illustrate a pipeline where an 'Image Encoder' (like a Vision Transformer) processes a picture and converts it into a sequence of 'visual tokens.' A common pitfall for learners is thinking that the model treats the image as a separate file it 'looks at.' I will correct this by showing how these visual tokens are interleaved directly with text tokens in the same transformer sequence. To the LLM’s brain, a 16x16 patch of pixels eventually looks just like another word. This explains why these models can 'reason' about images—they are using the same attention mechanisms we studied in Unit 2 to find relationships between visual patches and textual descriptors.

We will pause for a brief thought exercise: I’ll ask the learners to propose how they would use a VLM to solve a real-world problem, such as a visually impaired user navigating a grocery store. This exercise is designed to reveal whether they understand the 'reasoning' aspect—can the model count the apples in the frame and compare them to a shopping list? It forces them to see the model as an agent that can interpret visual state, not just a labeler. 

Finally, we will address the complexities of cross-modal alignment. I will explain that while we can align vision and text, adding audio or video adds layers of temporal complexity (time). I will wrap up by emphasizing that 'multimodality' is the path toward 'General' AI because it allows the model to verify linguistic concepts against physical reality. I'll warn against the 'alignment gap'—the danger where a model might recognize a 'hammer' visually but fail to understand its functional use in text if the joint space isn't perfectly mapped. This sets the stage for our next session on the limits of these models, as we question if seeing a hammer is the same as knowing how to use one.

tasks: Describe the process of cross-modal alignment using a joint embedding space.
Propose a practical application for a Vision-Language Model (VLM).

sessions.title: What Generative Models Can and Cannot Do
sessions.description: This session provides a reality check on current LLM limitations, including lack of world-state tracking and stochastic nature. You will learn to distinguish between 'emergent' reasoning and sophisticated pattern matching. This critical thinking skill is necessary to manage stakeholder expectations and design safe systems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
This session serves as the essential 'reality check' for the entire first unit. We begin by positioning Large Language Models (LLMs) not as sentient minds, but as incredibly sophisticated probability engines. The core pedagogical goal is to move the learner from seeing AI as a 'magic box' to understanding it as a 'system of prediction.' We start by drawing a distinction between 'World Knowledge'—the facts encoded in the model's weights—and 'World State'—the actual awareness of physical reality. Using the whiteboard, we will sketch a simple scenario, such as a cat sitting on a mat, and contrast how a human understands the physics of that scene versus how an LLM merely understands the statistical likelihood of the word 'mat' following 'cat.' This sets the stage for identifying why models 'hallucinate': they are forced to produce a likely sequence of tokens even when they lack the underlying data to support a factual claim.

Next, we tackle the concept of 'Stochastic Parrots' versus 'Emergent Reasoning.' This is the most critical intellectual hurdle of the session. We will visualize the 'Stochastic' nature by showing a probability distribution over a specific prompt, explaining that the model is essentially a mirror reflecting the patterns of its training data. To bridge this into practice, we introduce the 'Logic Puzzle' exercise. By presenting a puzzle that requires multiple steps of deduction—and showing a classic failure where the model shortcuts to a common but incorrect pattern found on the internet—we demonstrate that the model often prioritizes pattern matching over genuine symbolic logic. This prevents the learner from over-relying on the model for critical decision-making without verification.

We then transition to the boundary of capabilities, focusing on the lack of a 'Feedback Loop' with physical reality. On the whiteboard, we illustrate the closed-loop nature of an LLM: Input -> Prediction -> Output. Unlike a human who can test a hypothesis in the real world, the model is trapped in its text-based universe. This explains why models can write flawless-looking code that fails to run or provide medical advice that ignores physiological constraints. We must emphasize to the learner that 'fluency' is not 'accuracy.' A common pitfall for students is assuming that because a model is articulate, it must be intelligent; we counteract this by showing examples of 'confident' hallucinations where the syntax is perfect but the semantics are nonsensical.

Finally, we close by discussing the 'Safety and Expectations' framework. This part of the lecture is designed to empower the learner as an engineer or developer. We discuss the 'Probability of Failure' not as a bug to be fixed, but as a feature of the architecture. By mapping out the limitations—such as context window limits, lack of true memory, and the tendency to 'sycophancy' (agreeing with the user even when the user is wrong)—we prepare the learner to design robust systems that include human-in-the-loop oversight or external verification tools like RAG. The session concludes with a look at AI safety through the lens of these limitations, arguing that understanding what a model *cannot* do is the first step in building a system that it *should* do.

tasks: Analyze a 'logic puzzle' failure case to identify the model's reasoning breakdown.
Define the 'Stochastic Parrot' argument and its relevance to AI safety.

projects.deliverable_increment: A preprocessing script and vector index file (.pkl or .json) capable of performing cosine similarity searches on document chunks.

Accurately describe the impact of tokenization on model behavior and cost.

units.title: The Transformer
units.description: Deconstruct the engine of the LLM revolution, moving from the mathematical mechanics of self-attention to the architectural design of modern Transformer blocks.

lectures.title: Attention
lectures.description: This lecture explains the revolutionary mechanism that allows models to focus on specific parts of an input sequence, solving the long-range dependency problem inherent in older neural networks.

sessions.title: Why Attention
sessions.description: This session introduces the limitations of Recurrent Neural Networks and the intuition behind looking at an entire sequence simultaneously. You will understand how the 'bottleneck' of fixed-length vectors is broken by allowing the model to weight different inputs dynamically. Mastering this shift is essential for understanding why modern generative models can maintain coherence over long passages of text.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a long, linear chain of boxes on the whiteboard to represent a Recurrent Neural Network (RNN). Explain that before the Transformer revolution, we tried to process language like a ticker tape—one word at a time. The core problem to highlight here is the 'forgetting' nature of this architecture. As the teacher, you should visualize a 'hidden state' vector moving from left to right, becoming increasingly 'blurry' as it travels. Use the metaphor of a whisper game: by the time the model reaches the end of a long paragraph, the nuances of the first sentence are almost entirely lost. This sets the stage for why we needed a fundamental shift in how machines 'read.'

Transition into the 'Vanishing Gradient' problem by showing the mathematical consequence of this linear chain. Explain that during training, the signal to correct an error at the end of the sentence has to travel all the way back to the beginning. Draw the gradient signal as a wave that gets smaller and smaller until it disappears. This is crucial because it explains why models used to struggle with long-range dependencies—not because they didn't 'see' the words, but because they couldn't learn the relationship between a subject at the start of a page and a verb at the end. Make sure to emphasize that this wasn't just a hardware limit; it was a fundamental architectural bottleneck of 'fixed-length' memory.

Now, introduce the 'Attention' intuition as the solution to this bottleneck. Instead of a linear chain, draw a cloud of words where every word has a direct line of sight to every other word. Use the sentence 'The bank of the river was muddy, so the hiker didn't go to the bank to deposit his check' as a working example. Ask the students to mentally circle the word 'bank' and then look for the words that tell them which 'bank' it is. On the whiteboard, draw thick lines from 'bank' to 'river' and 'muddy' for the first instance, and to 'deposit' and 'check' for the second. This visualization demonstrates that meaning is not static; it is 'attended' to based on context.

Explain that 'Attention' effectively turns a sequence into a search-and-retrieval problem. Instead of trying to squeeze the entire history of a sentence into a single vector, the model creates a dynamic map of relevance for every single token. Address a common misconception here: students often think attention is just 'looking at everything at once.' Clarify that it is actually about 'selective focus'—the model decides which words are worth ignoring and which are vital for the current calculation. This shift from sequential processing to parallel, weighted focus is what allowed LLMs to finally master the coherence and logic seen in modern generative AI.

Conclude the session with a reflective practice moment. Ask the students to consider how they would identify the referent of the word 'it' in a complex sentence. This exercise is designed to reveal if they understand that 'Attention' is a mechanism for disambiguation. By the end of this session, the learner should feel the frustration of the RNN's 'memory loss' and the relief provided by the Transformer's 'global vision,' preparing them for the mathematical mechanics of QKV in the next session.

tasks: Identify the 'vanishing gradient' problem in a sample RNN structure.
Explain how a human reader 'attends' to specific words when disambiguating the word 'bank' in a sentence.

sessions.title: Self-Attention and Query-Key-Value
sessions.description: This session breaks down the mathematical core of the Transformer: the Query, Key, and Value (QKV) vectors. You will learn how to compute dot-product attention and how these vectors interact to retrieve information from the sequence. This provides the mathematical foundation necessary to move beyond metaphors and understand how silicon actually 'thinks' about context.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this whiteboard session by acknowledging the 'black box' problem: we know models understand context, but how do they actually quantify it? To transition from the high-level intuition of the previous session to mathematical reality, I will introduce the analogy of a database retrieval system. In a standard database, you have a specific key and you get a specific value. In the Transformer world, we want something more fluid—a 'fuzzy' retrieval. I will draw three distinct vectors on the board for a single token: Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V). The 'Query' represents what the current word is looking for; the 'Key' represents what the word contains; and the 'Value' is the actual information it contributes to the next layer. The crucial point to emphasize here is that these aren't just labels—they are linear transformations of the same input embedding, meaning the model learns three different 'personalities' for every word.

Next, I will visualize the 'Attention Score' calculation using a dot-product operation between the Query of word A and the Key of word B. On the board, I'll illustrate this as a physical alignment: if two vectors point in the same direction, the score is high; if they are orthogonal, the score is zero. This is where I address the common misconception that attention is just 'importance.' It is actually 'compatibility.' I will walk through a 2-word example, such as 'Green' and 'Apple.' We'll calculate the raw score of 'Apple' (Query) looking at 'Green' (Key). Students often struggle with why we need both Q and K. I’ll explain that by separating them, we allow a word to be highly 'attractive' to others (a strong Key) without necessarily needing to 'look' at others (a strong Query) in the same way.

Once we have the raw scores, I will introduce the Scaling and Softmax step. I’ll write the formula for Scaled Dot-Product Attention, explaining that the division by the square root of the dimension (dk) is a safety valve to prevent gradients from vanishing or exploding when numbers get too large. Then, I will draw a Softmax curve to show how it forces all our raw compatibility scores to sum to 1. This transforms our raw math into a probability distribution. This is a perfect moment for a practice break: I’ll provide two sets of numbers and ask the students to predict which word will dominate the attention 'budget' after Softmax. This reveals whether they understand that Softmax is a 'winner-takes-most' operation that filters out noise.

Finally, we arrive at the 'Value' (V) projection. This is the 'payload' phase. I will show how the Softmax weights act as a blender: we take 80% of the Value from Word A and 20% of the Value from Word B to create a new, context-aware representation. This is the 'Aha!' moment where the student sees that the output is no longer just the word 'Apple,' but 'Apple-in-the-context-of-Green.' I will wrap up by warning about the quadratic complexity trap: as the sequence gets longer, every token has to produce a Q to check every other token's K, which explains why LLM context windows have physical and computational limits.

tasks: Calculate a raw attention score for a 2-word sequence using provided Q and K vectors.
Describe the role of the Softmax function in normalizing attention weights.

sessions.title: Multi-Head Attention
sessions.description: This session explores how running multiple attention mechanisms in parallel allows the model to capture different types of relationships, such as grammar versus semantics. You will learn to visualize 'heads' attending to different linguistic features simultaneously. This layer of complexity explains the expressive power of LLMs and how they manage multi-faceted meaning.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the limitation of a single focus. If the core of attention is to compute a single 'weighted average' of context, explain that a single set of Q, K, and V weights can only look for one thing at a time—much like a person trying to read a sentence while simultaneously checking for grammatical errors, emotional tone, and factual accuracy using only one eye. The most important idea here is that language is multi-dimensional; a word like 'bank' has a relationship with 'river' (semantic) but also a relationship with the word 'the' (syntactic). We need more than one 'filter' to capture these layers.

Transition to the whiteboard to visualize the concept of 'Heads.' Instead of performing one large attention calculation, we split the embedding space into multiple smaller subspaces. Use a diagram where a 512-dimensional vector is sliced into 8 smaller 64-dimensional pieces. Explain that each 'head' is a complete, independent attention mechanism with its own learned weight matrices. This allows Head 1 to focus on 'who did what' (subject-verb agreement), while Head 2 might focus on 'where did it happen' (prepositional phrases). The logic is that by ensemble-ing these different perspectives, the model gains a panoramic view of the text rather than a tunnel-visioned one.

Address a common misconception: students often think that more heads simply mean more 'power' in a linear sense. Clarify that the total dimensionality usually remains the same—we are just reallocating our representational budget. To illustrate this, walk through the 'Concatenation and Projection' step. Once each head has finished its individual calculation, we end up with multiple smaller output vectors. We must 'glue' them back together. Draw a horizontal stack of the 8 output vectors and then show a final linear layer (the 'Output Projection') that blends them back into a single vector of the original size. This final step is crucial because it allows the model to decide how to weigh the opinions of different heads before passing the information to the next layer.

Introduce a practice moment by asking the learners to consider a specific sentence: 'The chef, who was trained in Paris, cooked a steak.' Guide them to see that a single attention head might focus on the proximity of 'Paris' to 'cooked,' while a different head might learn to leapfrog over the middle clause to connect 'chef' directly to 'cooked.' This reveals the power of multi-head attention in handling long-range dependencies and complex nested structures.

Conclude the session by emphasizing that this architecture is what makes Transformers 'general purpose.' Because we don't hard-code what each head should look for, the training process naturally specializes them. One head might become a 'comma-checker' while another becomes a 'pronoun-resolver.' This self-organizing property is the secret behind the emergent linguistic intelligence of LLMs. Remind the learners that without this parallel processing, the model would be a 'jack of all trades, master of none,' unable to resolve the intricate nuances that define human language.

tasks: Explain why a single attention head might struggle to capture both syntactic structure and topical relevance.
Diagram the concatenation and linear projection step in a multi-head attention block.

sessions.title: Positional Information
sessions.description: Since Transformers process tokens in parallel, they are 'order-blind' by default; this session teaches you how positional encodings inject word-order back into the system. You will understand the use of sine and cosine functions or learned embeddings to represent sequence position. This is a critical technical detail for understanding why LLMs can follow instructions where word order is paramount.
sessions.sessionOutline:
The core paradox of the Transformer is its 'set-based' nature: by treating tokens as a parallel batch to maximize GPU efficiency, the model inherently forgets that language has a specific sequence. This session begins by visualizing the 'Bag of Words' problem. If we feed 'The cat chased the dog' and 'The dog chased the cat' into the self-attention mechanism we've just studied, the attention scores between 'cat' and 'chased' would be identical in both scenarios because the dot-product operation doesn't know where a vector sits in the list. This realization is crucial; we must explain that without a 'time stamp' or 'address' for each token, the model is grammatically blind, unable to distinguish between a subject and an object. 

To solve this, we introduce the concept of Positional Encodings as a 'top-up' to the semantic embedding. Rather than concatenating a position ID (which might disrupt the vector space), we add a positional vector directly to the word vector. This is a delicate operation. I will explain that the positional signal must be strong enough to be noticed by the model but subtle enough not to drown out the word's meaning. We'll use the analogy of a transparent overlay on a map: the map shows the terrain (the word meaning), while the overlay provides the latitude and longitude (the position). This 'addition' works because high-dimensional vector spaces can represent multiple independent features simultaneously, a phenomenon known as superposition.

Next, we dive into the 'Why' behind the Sine and Cosine functions used in the original 'Attention is All You Need' paper. Instead of just listing formulas, the focus here is on the property of 'Relative Relationships.' By using periodic functions with varying frequencies, the model doesn't just learn that a token is at 'Index 5'; it learns that 'Index 5' is a specific distance from 'Index 3.' I'll describe how these waves create a unique fingerprint for every position that allows the model to calculate relative distances through linear transformations. A common learner pitfall is thinking these are 'learned' weights; I must clarify that these are fixed geometric patterns, though modern models sometimes opt for 'Learned Positional Embeddings' where the model treats each index like a vocabulary word.

We will then pivot to the practical evolution of this concept: Relative Positional Encodings and RoPE (Rotary Positional Embeddings). I will explain that while absolute positions tell you where you are in the whole book, relative positions tell you how far the 'verb' is from the 'noun.' This is why models like Llama can handle longer contexts than they were trained on—they understand the 'rotation' of vectors relative to one another rather than just a fixed starting point. This transition is vital for students to understand why context window limits exist and how we are engineering our way around them.

The session concludes with a mental simulation exercise. I'll ask the students to predict the outcome of a 'scrambled' sentence. If we remove positional encodings, why does 'The cat chased the dog' produce the same hidden states as 'dog the chased cat the'? By forcing them to visualize the attention matrix as a permutation-invariant operation, they grasp that positional information isn't a 'nice-to-have'—it's the only thing preventing the most powerful AI in the world from regressing into a simple keyword search engine. This bridge between the 'spatial' math and 'temporal' language structure is the final piece of the Transformer's core architecture.

tasks: Differentiate between absolute and relative positional encodings.
Predict how a model's output would change if positional encodings were removed from a sentence like 'The cat chased the dog'.

lectures.title: Architecture
lectures.description: In this lecture, we assemble the individual attention mechanisms into a complete Transformer block and examine how these blocks are stacked and specialized into different model families.

sessions.title: The Transformer Block
sessions.description: This session covers the standard layout of a Transformer layer, including the feed-forward networks that follow the attention mechanism. You will be able to trace the flow of data through a single block, from input to output. Understanding this repeating unit is key to grasping how LLMs scale to hundreds of layers.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by zooming out from the individual math operations to view the Transformer block as a modular 'processing unit.' The core pedagogical goal is to help learners see the Transformer not as a chaotic mess of layers, but as a repeatable, elegant template. I start by drawing a large rectangular container on the whiteboard, labeling it 'The Transformer Block.' I emphasize that this block is the DNA of the model—whether we are talking about a small BERT model or a massive GPT-4, this internal structure remains remarkably consistent. The first concept to establish is the sequential hand-off: the data enters as a representation of meaning (embeddings), gets contextualized by the attention mechanism, and is then refined by the Feed-Forward Network (FFN).

The first critical drawing on the whiteboard is the 'Residual Highway.' Before detailing the Attention or FFN, I draw two vertical paths: a straight line that goes from bottom to top (the residual connection) and a branched path that goes through the sub-layers. I explain that the attention mechanism acts like a 'social mixer'—it's where tokens talk to each other to figure out context. However, I make sure to warn students of a common misconception: that attention does all the work. In reality, the attention layer only moves information around; it doesn't actually 'process' or 'store' complex patterns about the world. This sets the stage for the next component.

Next, I sketch the Position-wise Feed-Forward Network (FFN) as the second major room in our block. This is the 'knowledge processing' center. I describe it as a series of dense layers that act on each token independently. The intuition to convey here is that if Attention is about 'relationships,' the FFN is about 'identity.' It's where the model uses its learned weights to transform the newly acquired context into a higher-level abstract concept. I'll use the example of the word 'Bank'—Attention identifies that the surrounding words are 'river' and 'water,' but the FFN is what actually transforms the internal vector to represent a 'geographical landmass' rather than a 'financial institution.'

I then pause for a 'Mental Sketch' exercise. I ask the students to visualize where the data would 'clog' if we removed the FFN. This reveals if they understand that without the FFN, the model would just keep shuffling tokens around without ever increasing the complexity of their internal representation. I clarify that the FFN typically has a much higher dimensionality (often 4x the model's hidden size) in its middle layer, which serves as a 'workspace' for the model to think before compressing the result back down.

Finally, we wrap up by looking at the 'Add & Norm' wrappers around both the Attention and FFN. I draw these as protective shells. I explain that these are the 'plumbing' that keeps the signals from exploding or vanishing as we stack 12, 24, or 96 of these blocks on top of each other. By the end of this session, the student should see the Transformer block as a two-stage engine: first, look around (Attention), and second, think about what you saw (FFN), all while keeping the original signal intact via the residual highway.

tasks: Sketch the components of a standard Transformer block in order.
Explain the role of the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) in processing the output of the attention layer.

sessions.title: Residuals and Normalization
sessions.description: This session explains the 'plumbing' of the architecture: Skip (Residual) connections and Layer Normalization. You will learn how these techniques stabilize training and prevent gradients from disappearing in deep networks. This technical insight explains why we can build 'Deep' models rather than just wide ones.
sessions.sessionOutline:
In this session, we transition from the high-level logic of attention to the 'unseen plumbing' that makes deep Transformers possible: Residual Connections and Layer Normalization. Start by posing a fundamental problem of deep learning: the vanishing gradient. Explain that while we want to build models with dozens or hundreds of layers to capture complex patterns, each additional layer acts like a lens that can distort or lose the signal coming from the loss function during training. This sets the stage for Residuals as the 'highway' that keeps the signal clear.

Visualize the Residual Connection (or Skip Connection) on the whiteboard as a bypass lane. Draw the attention mechanism as a complex processing unit, but show a parallel line that carries the original input directly to the output, where they are added together ($Output = x + Sublayer(x)$). Explain that the core idea here is 'learning the difference.' Instead of the network having to learn an entirely new representation from scratch at every layer, it only has to learn what needs to change or be added to the current state. This intuition is vital: it reduces the burden on the weights and prevents the model from getting 'lost' in its own complexity. Address the common misconception that residuals are just a 'backup'; emphasize that they allow the gradient to flow backward through the network almost unimpeded, which is why we can train 100-layer models today instead of being stuck at 10 layers.

Next, introduce Layer Normalization (LayerNorm) as the stabilizer that keeps the numbers within a healthy range. On the whiteboard, contrast this with Batch Normalization, which many students with a computer vision background might know. Explain why Batch Norm fails in NLP: because sentence lengths vary and the statistics of a 'batch' in language are often too noisy. Draw a diagram showing a matrix of activations where LayerNorm calculates the mean and variance across the features of a single token rather than across different examples in a batch. Explain that this makes the model's training much more robust to the specific scale of the input embeddings and the internal weights. It’s the difference between a car that shakes violently as it goes faster versus one with a high-end suspension system.

Conclude by integrating these two concepts into the 'Pre-LN' vs 'Post-LN' debate. Show where these components sit in the actual Transformer block. Most modern architectures (like GPT and Llama) use Pre-Normalization, where the signal is normalized before entering the attention or feed-forward layers. Explain that this further stabilizes training by ensuring the input to every sub-layer is consistently distributed. Use a practice moment here: ask the students to consider what would happen if we removed the residual connection but kept the normalization. This helps them realize that without the skip connection, the normalization would still be trying to fix a signal that is fundamentally decaying or exploding, reinforcing the symbiotic relationship between these two 'plumbing' features.

tasks: Contrast Layer Normalization with Batch Normalization in the context of sequence processing.
Explain how residual connections allow gradients to bypass non-linearities during backpropagation.

sessions.title: Encoder, Decoder, and Model Families
sessions.description: This session distinguishes between Encoder-only (like BERT), Decoder-only (like GPT), and Encoder-Decoder (like T5) architectures. You will learn which architecture is best for specific tasks like classification versus generation. This mapping is vital for choosing the right base model for your future AI applications.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the lecture by drawing a fundamental distinction between 'understanding' and 'predicting.' Use the whiteboard to illustrate the original Transformer as a 'bridge' between two languages. Explain that while the core components (attention and feed-forward layers) are consistent across all models, how we arrange them determines the model's 'personality' and its ultimate use case. The goal here is to shift the student's mindset from seeing a single 'Transformer' to recognizing it as a modular kit that can be assembled into different shapes: the Encoder-only, the Decoder-only, and the Encoder-Decoder.

Draw the 'Encoder-only' block first (referencing BERT). Visualize this as a 'bi-directional' processor where every token can 'see' every other token in the sequence. Explain the logic: if you want to classify a sentence's sentiment or extract named entities, you want the model to have the full context of the entire sentence at once. This is the 'all-seeing eye' approach. A common mistake students make is assuming this is good for generation; emphasize that because there is no masking, an encoder-only model struggles to generate text word-by-word because it doesn't have a natural direction of flow.

Contrast this immediately with the 'Decoder-only' architecture (referencing GPT and Llama). This is the 'Causal' model. On the whiteboard, draw the mask—a triangular block that prevents a token from looking at the 'future.' Explain why this is the engine of modern generative AI: by forcing the model to only look at what came before, we train it to be a master of the 'next token prediction' game. This is the most important takeaway of the session: the 'causal mask' is what creates the illusion of creativity and flow. Use the example of writing a story; if the model could see the end of the sentence while writing the beginning, it wouldn't learn how to actually build the bridge from A to B.

Introduce the 'Encoder-Decoder' (referencing T5) as the hybrid solution. Illustrate how the Encoder processes a source (like a French sentence) and the Decoder generates the target (the English translation) while 'cross-attending' to the Encoder's maps. This is a crucial moment to discuss efficiency: why use two parts when GPT can do it with one? Explain that for specific tasks like translation or summarization, having a dedicated 'comprehension' unit (Encoder) and a dedicated 'production' unit (Decoder) can often lead to higher quality results than a general-purpose model.

Transition to a practice moment by listing several real-world tasks on the board: 'Is this email spam?', 'Write a poem about a cat', and 'Translate this manual into Japanese.' Ask the students to map these to the model families. This exercise is designed to reveal whether they understand the 'directionality' of information flow. If they choose a Decoder-only for spam detection, acknowledge that it works, but guide them toward why an Encoder-only (BERT) might be more efficient for that specific classification task.

Finally, wrap up by contextualizing where the industry is today. While BERT was the king of the late 2010s, the world has shifted heavily toward 'Decoder-only' (the GPT/Llama family) because of the scaling properties and the flexibility of 'Prompting.' This sets the stage for future sessions by showing that architecture choices aren't just academic—they dictate how we interact with the AI (through prompts versus through task-specific training).

tasks: Categorize popular models (Llama, BERT, T5) into their respective architectural families.
Explain why GPT models use a 'causal' mask in their self-attention layers.

sessions.title: Scaling the Architecture
sessions.description: This session discusses how changing the width (embedding dimension) and depth (number of layers) affects model capacity. You will understand the relationship between parameter count and the emergence of new capabilities. This knowledge prepares you for the 'Scaling Laws' discussion in the next unit by framing the physical dimensions of the model.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the Transformer not just as a mathematical function, but as a physical object with dimensions: depth and width. In this 'whiteboard' session, I will draw a rectangular box representing the model. The vertical axis represents 'Depth' (number of layers, L), and the horizontal axis represents 'Width' (the embedding dimension, d_model). The core idea to land here is that 'Scaling' isn't just making things bigger; it's about increasing the capacity for the model to store and process information. I will use the analogy of a library: depth is the number of floors (how many times the data is refined), while width is the size of the bookshelves on each floor (how many distinct features can be captured simultaneously).

Next, we transition to the 'Parameter Math' to demystify where the billions of parameters actually live. I’ll start by sketching a single Transformer block and highlighting the two main regions: the Attention mechanism and the Feed-Forward Network (FFN). I’ll walk through the calculation—explaining that most parameters reside in the weight matrices (the Q, K, V, and Output projections, plus the two massive layers in the FFN). It’s crucial to show that if you double the width (d_model), the number of parameters roughly quadruples because of the matrix operations (d_model squared). This explains why wider models are exponentially more 'expensive' in terms of memory. I will pause here for a quick mental check: 'If we keep the total parameters the same, would you rather have a very deep, narrow model or a shallow, wide one?' This triggers a discussion on the trade-offs between sequential processing (depth) and representational richness (width).

We then move into the 'Emergent Capabilities' part of the lecture. This is where I explain the 'Why' behind scaling. I’ll plot a conceptual graph on the board showing performance (error rate) versus scale. I want to highlight that as we increase these dimensions, the model doesn't just get better at what it already does; it starts to exhibit new behaviors, like zero-shot reasoning or complex coding. A common misconception for learners at this stage is thinking that more parameters automatically equal more intelligence. I will correct this by explaining that 'Scale' is a prerequisite for these behaviors, but the data quality and training duration (which we will cover in the next unit) must keep pace. I’ll frame this as the 'Physical Limit' of what a model can possibly learn.

Finally, we address the 'Hardware Reality'—the ceiling that stops us from building infinite-scale models. I will draw a representation of GPU VRAM (Video RAM). I’ll explain that 'Depth' is particularly tricky because, during training, we have to store the activations for every single layer to perform backpropagation. This creates a memory bottleneck. I will use the visualization of 'Gradient Checkpointing' as a way engineers try to cheat this limit, but emphasize that ultimately, the physical memory of the hardware dictates the maximum dimensions of our architecture. The session ends with a hands-on calculation exercise: given a specific d_model and number of layers, the students will estimate the memory footprint. This transforms the session from abstract theory into the practical engineering constraints they will face in production.

tasks: Calculate the approximate number of parameters in a simplified Transformer block given hidden dimensions.
Identify the hardware constraints that usually limit the maximum depth of a model.

lectures.title: Inference
lectures.description: This lecture focuses on the runtime behavior of the model, specifically how it turns internal probabilities into human-readable text and why this process sometimes fails.

sessions.title: Greedy, Beam, and Sampling Decoding
sessions.description: This session introduces the different strategies for selecting the next token from the model's output distribution.
