You will learn the trade-offs between 'Greedy' search (fast but repetitive) and 'Beam' search (comprehensive but slow). This allows you to control the 'creativity' and logic of your generative outputs.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by drawing a simple probability distribution on the board for the next token after the phrase 'The capital of France is'. This visual sets the stage for everything that follows: the model doesn't output 'Paris' directly; it outputs a giant list of numbers for every word it knows. Explain that 'Decoding' is simply the rulebook we use to decide which word actually gets written onto the screen. This is a critical concept-first moment: the 'intelligence' is in the distribution, but the 'personality' and 'accuracy' are in the decoding strategy.

Begin the 'Greedy Search' walkthrough by drawing a decision tree where we always pick the tallest bar in the histogram. Use the example of a repetitive loop, like 'I like to code, I like to code, I like to...' to show why greedy search often fails. It’s shortsighted. It chooses the best immediate word but might lead the model into a local minimum where it gets stuck in a loop or produces a very boring, generic sentence. This explains the 'Greedy' name—it takes what looks best right now without a plan for the future.

Transition to 'Beam Search' by asking the students, 'What if we kept our options open?' On the whiteboard, branch out the decision tree to show two or three parallel paths (the 'beams'). Illustrate how a word that looks slightly less likely at step one might lead to a much higher overall sequence probability by step four. This is essential for tasks like translation where the grammar of the whole sentence matters more than the first word. A common pitfall for students is thinking more beams always equals better results; explain that too many beams often lead to 'generic' or 'safe' text that lacks human-like flair.

Introduce 'Sampling' as the antidote to the robotic nature of Greedy and Beam search. Explain that instead of picking the highest probability, we roll a die weighted by those probabilities. This is where 'creativity' comes from. Use the practice task of step-by-step decoding here: give the students a small table of three words and their probabilities (e.g., Apple 0.7, Banana 0.2, Zebra 0.1). Ask them what Greedy would pick every single time versus what might happen if we sampled. This reveals the core tension in LLMs: the trade-off between the 'factually correct' path and the 'creative' path.

Conclude by contrasting these methods against real-world use cases. Use the board to map a spectrum: on the far left, place 'Fact-based/Translation' (Beam Search), and on the far right, place 'Storytelling/Chat' (Sampling). This gives the students a mental framework for the upcoming sessions on Temperature and Top-p, as they now understand that the choice of decoding strategy is a deliberate engineering decision based on the desired output behavior.

tasks: Perform a step-by-step greedy decoding on a sample probability distribution.
Explain why beam search is more commonly used in translation than in creative writing.

sessions.title: Temperature and Top-p
sessions.description: This session explains the hyperparameters that govern randomness in LLMs, such as Temperature, Top-k, and Top-p (Nucleus) sampling. You will learn how to tune these values to prevent the model from becoming too predictable or too chaotic. Mastery of these settings is the first step toward professional prompt engineering and model control.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by illustrating the 'Softmax' output of the model as a probability distribution. Explain that while the model outputs raw numbers (logits), these are squashed into probabilities that sum to 1.0. This is the moment to introduce Temperature as the 'volume knob' for the model's confidence. Visually contrast a cold distribution (Temperature < 1) where one peak is extremely high, versus a hot distribution (Temperature > 1) where the probability mass is spread more evenly across all tokens. The core idea here is that the model doesn't just know what is 'correct'; it knows the relative likelihood of everything else, and we can manipulate how much it 'listens' to those low-probability outliers.

Deepen the intuition by explaining the mathematical effect of Temperature: it's a scaling factor applied to the logits before the Softmax function. If you set the temperature very low (e.g., 0.1), you are effectively telling the model to 'bet the house' on the most likely word, leading to repetitive or overly safe text. If you push it past 1.0, you are artificially boosting the underdog tokens. This is where you should warn about 'Gibberish'—the common pitfall where a model starts outputting random punctuation or symbols because the temperature is so high that meaningful words and noise become equally likely.

Transition from Temperature to 'Top-k' and 'Top-p' (Nucleus Sampling) by framing them as 'safety filters.' Explain that while Temperature shifts the probabilities, Top-k and Top-p cut the distribution tail off entirely. Use a list of potential next words for the phrase 'The cat sat on the...' to demonstrate. If 'mat' is 40% and 'moon' is 0.01%, Top-k might keep only the top 10 words, while Top-p (set to 0.9) keeps the dynamic set of words whose cumulative probability reaches 90%. This is the critical distinction: Top-p is 'aware' of the distribution's shape. In certain contexts, there are only two logical next words; in others, there are twenty. Top-p scales to fit the confidence of the model.

Introduce a practice moment where students must calculate a Top-p cutoff. Give them a distribution like {A: 0.5, B: 0.3, C: 0.15, D: 0.05}. Ask them which tokens remain if p=0.7 (A and B) versus if p=0.9 (A, B, and C). This exercise is designed to reveal if they understand that Top-p is an 'inclusive sum' rather than a fixed number of items. This helps engineers understand why their models might suddenly stop being 'creative' even with high temperature—because a restrictive Top-p might be pruning all the interesting, diverse choices before they even have a chance to be sampled.

Conclude by discussing the 'Goldilocks Zone' of sampling. Emphasize that there is no universal 'perfect' setting. For factual tasks like code generation or data extraction, lean toward low temperature and low p (or greedy decoding). For creative writing or brainstorming, lean toward higher temperature (0.7-1.0) and a wider Top-p (0.9-0.95). The goal of this session is to move the student from 'randomly clicking buttons' to 'deliberate calibration' based on the specific behavior they need the LLM to exhibit. Address the misconception that higher temperature equals 'smarter' output; it simply equals more variance, which can lead to brilliance or total breakdown.

tasks: Explain how a temperature > 1.0 flattens the probability distribution.
Given a distribution, determine which tokens would be included in a Top-p (p=0.9) cutoff.

sessions.title: Speed, Caching, and Batching
sessions.description: This session dives into the engineering of inference, focusing on the KV-Cache and how it avoids redundant computations during generation. You will understand why the first token takes longer to generate than subsequent ones. This is critical for building responsive, cost-effective applications in production.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by addressing the 'waiting' experience in LLM interaction. Draw a simple horizontal timeline on the whiteboard representing the life of a single user request. Mark the moment the user hits enter and the moment the first token appears. This is 'Time to First Token' (TTFT). Then, mark the steady cadence of subsequent tokens. The core goal of this session is to explain why LLMs are 'autoregressive'—meaning they generate one token at a time—and how this sequential nature creates a massive computational bottleneck that we solve with caching and batching.

Transition into the mechanics of the Transformer's attention mechanism from the previous lectures. On the whiteboard, draw the Query (Q), Key (K), and Value (V) matrices for a sequence of 10 tokens. Explain that for every new token generated, the model has to look back at all previous tokens to calculate their relevance. Without optimization, the model would re-calculate the Key and Value vectors for the entire conversation history every single time a new word is added. This is the 'Redundancy Trap.' Explain that this is like reading an entire book from page one every time you want to read the next sentence. This visualization helps students grasp that the cost of generation grows quadratically with the length of the text unless we find a way to 'remember' the past.

Introduce the 'KV-Cache' as the primary engineering solution. Draw a box labeled 'GPU Memory' and show how, after we calculate the K and V vectors for token #1, we store them in this cache. For token #2, we only need to compute its own K and V and then 'concatenate' them with the cached vectors from token #1. This turns a repetitive, heavy matrix multiplication into a retrieval and update task. Emphasize that the KV-Cache is why the first token (pre-fill phase) is computationally 'heavier' than the others: the model has to process the entire input prompt at once to populate the cache, whereas subsequent tokens (decoding phase) only process a single new token.

Address the 'Memory-Speed Tradeoff' to prevent the common misconception that caching is a free lunch. Explicitly state that the KV-Cache lives in high-speed GPU VRAM, which is a finite and expensive resource. If a model has 70 billion parameters and a massive context window, the KV-Cache can quickly consume dozens of gigabytes of memory. This is the moment to introduce a 'Capacity Crisis' scenario: if your cache is full, you can't serve more users or process longer documents. This bridges the gap from theoretical math to the hardware reality that engineers face in production.

Finally, move to 'Batching' and 'Throughput.' On the board, draw a single lane of traffic versus a multi-lane highway. Explain that GPUs are massively parallel processors that hate being idle. If we process one user at a time, the GPU is mostly 'waiting' for data to move. By batching multiple user requests together, we maximize 'Throughput' (tokens per second across all users), but we might increase 'Latency' (the wait time for a specific user). Use a whiteboard diagram to show how the GPU handles a matrix of multiple requests simultaneously. Conclude by challenging students to think about the tension between making a chatbot feel 'snappy' for one person versus making it 'cheap' to run for a million people.

tasks: Describe the purpose of the KV-Cache in an autoregressive decoder.
Explain the impact of batch size on inference throughput versus individual request latency.

sessions.title: Why Models Hallucinate
sessions.description: This session bridges the gap between architecture and behavior by examining the root causes of hallucinations, such as the 'probabilistic' nature of the model and training data noise. You will learn to recognize when a model is 'confabulating' versus 'reasoning'. Understanding this limitation is fundamental for any developer looking to deploy LLMs safely in the real world.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by reframing the LLM not as a database, but as a statistical mimic. To ground the students, I will draw a diagram on the whiteboard showing two distinct paths: 'Reasoning' (connecting logical nodes) versus 'Token-level Probability' (following the strongest statistical signal). The core objective of this session is to bridge the architectural reality of the Transformer with the behavioral flaw of hallucinations. I will explain that 'hallucination' is actually a misnomer; the model is always doing the same thing—predicting the next likely token—but we call it a hallucination when that prediction deviates from external reality. This sets the stage for understanding that the model has no concept of 'truth,' only 'likelihood.'

Next, I will move to the whiteboard to illustrate the 'Objective Function Conflict.' I’ll write down the standard training goal: 'Maximize the likelihood of the next token in the training set.' I will then present a hypothetical scenario where the model is asked a question about a niche fact that wasn't in its training data. I'll draw a probability distribution curve showing how the model, forced by its architecture to produce a token, chooses a 'plausible-sounding' path. This is the 'fluent liar' problem. The most important takeaway here is that the model's fluency is its own worst enemy; because it is trained on human-like text, it learns the *style* of authority without the *substance* of fact-checking.

To address a common misconception, I will explain that hallucinations aren't just 'forgetting'—they are often 'over-generalizing.' Using a visual metaphor of a neural network's weights as a compressed map, I'll show how similar concepts (e.g., two different CEOs of the same company) can bleed together in the high-dimensional embedding space. When the model 'retrieves' information, it’s actually reconstructing it from these fuzzy weights. If the reconstruction is slightly off, the result is a plausible falsehood. I will emphasize that this is a feature of lossy compression, not a bug that can be 'fixed' with a simple patch, which helps students understand why RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) becomes necessary in later units.

We will then transition to an 'Observation Moment' where I present a sample model response that contains a subtle error—for example, a biography where the birth date is off by three years. I will ask the students to trace why a 'probability-maximizing' machine would make that specific error. This exercise is designed to reveal that the model often defaults to 'template-matching' (e.g., 'most famous people were born in the 1950s') when its specific weights for that entity are weak. It teaches them to look for 'stochastic parrots' behavior in their own outputs.

Finally, I will conclude by discussing 'Data Contamination' and 'Noise.' I'll sketch out how contradictory information in the training set (the internet) forces the model to learn multiple 'truths.' When a user prompts the model, it isn't 'lying'; it is simply navigating a contradictory probability landscape. I'll end the session by positioning the developer's role: since we cannot stop the model from being probabilistic, we must build guardrails and validation layers. This provides a direct pedagogical bridge to Unit 5, where we will learn to use 'LLM-as-a-Judge' to detect these very failures we've just visualized.

tasks: Identify a hallucination in a sample model response and trace it back to a potential lack of ground truth in weights.
Discuss how the objective function of 'maximizing likelihood' can lead to plausible-sounding falsehoods.

exams.title: The Transformer Architecture & Inference Exam
exams.goal: Evaluate the learner's understanding of self-attention mechanics, transformer block components, and the technical nuances of the decoding process.
sections: Comprehensive assessment covering the QKV mechanism, positional encoding, encoder vs decoder differences, and the impact of decoding parameters (Temperature, Top-p) on model output.
successCriteria: Accurately describe the computation flow of a self-attention head.
Differentiate between model families based on their structural design.
Predict the effect of specific decoding strategies on output diversity and coherence.
Explain how the KV-cache optimizes inference performance.

units.title: Training and Adaptation
units.description: Explore how models are pretrained on massive datasets and subsequently aligned for human interaction through fine-tuning and Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF).

lectures.title: Pretraining
lectures.description: This lecture covers the massive-scale initial phase of model creation, focusing on the data, the computational limits, and the mathematical laws that govern how model performance scales with resources.

sessions.title: Pretraining Data
sessions.description: In this session, you will explore the composition of datasets used to train LLMs, including Common Crawl, specialized code datasets, and curated books. You will learn how the quality and diversity of training data dictate the model's fundamental world knowledge, which is essential for understanding why models sometimes reflect specific biases or lack niche information.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing the Large Language Model not as a 'brain,' but as a high-fidelity mirror of human digital output. To understand why a model behaves the way it does, we must look at the 'raw ingredients' of its pretraining. On the whiteboard, I will start by drawing a massive funnel. At the top, I’ll label the messy, uncurated internet—specifically 'Common Crawl'—and at the bottom, the compressed intelligence of the model weights. The core idea here is that pretraining is a game of data curation, not just data collection. I'll explain that while the internet provides the scale needed for deep learning, most of it is 'noise' (HTML tags, gibberish, spam) that provides zero semantic value for learning language patterns.

Next, we shift the visualization to a 'Nutrition Label' for a model like Llama or GPT-3. I will sketch out the primary food groups: Web Text (the breadth), Books (the depth of reasoning and narrative), and Code (the logic). It’s crucial to emphasize why we include code even for models that aren't primarily 'coding assistants.' The teacher should explain the logic chain: code is the most structured form of human language we have; by learning to predict the next token in Python or C++, the model learns 'reasoning' and 'dependency' in a way that informal chat logs cannot provide. This prevents the common misconception that models only learn facts; they are actually learning the underlying structure of logical sequences.

To make the concept of data quality visceral, I'll introduce an interactive 'Filtering Challenge.' I will write a hypothetical snippet of raw web text on the board—filled with toxic comments, boilerplate legal disclaimers, and broken encoding characters—and ask the students to play 'Data Engineer.' We will circle what needs to be removed. This exercise is designed to reveal the invisible labor behind LLMs: deduplication and quality filtering. If we don't deduplicate, the model might memorize a specific repetitive phrase from the web and become 'stuck' on it during generation, a phenomenon known as the 'Boring Model' problem. This connects the abstract idea of a dataset back to the practical behavior of the model in production.

Finally, we will address the 'World Knowledge' vs. 'Bias' trade-off. I’ll draw a map of the world on the board and shade areas representing the English-speaking internet vs. other languages. This serves as a visual diagnostic for why LLMs are Western-centric and may hallucinate cultural facts for underrepresented regions. The takeaway for the students must be that a model’s 'truth' is bounded by its training corpus. If the pretraining data is 90% English, its 'logic' will inherently follow English syntax and cultural norms. We conclude by stressing that understanding the data mix is the first step in diagnosing model failure later in the course—if it wasn't in the pretraining data, the model hasn't truly 'learned' it; it is just guessing based on statistical proximity.

tasks: Analyze a sample of raw web text and identify potential noise and quality issues that would need filtering for pretraining.
Categorize the data sources used in a major model like GPT-3 or Llama and explain the purpose of each category.

sessions.title: Scaling Laws
sessions.description: You will study the empirical power laws that relate model size, dataset size, and compute budget to final model performance. By understanding the Chinchilla scaling laws, you will gain the ability to predict whether a model is bottlenecked by its parameters or its data, a critical skill for any researcher or engineer planning a training run.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the central engineering dilemma of the pretraining era: if you are given a fixed budget of millions of dollars in compute, how do you decide whether to build a bigger brain or feed it more books? This is where we introduce the 'Scaling Laws' as the foundational physics of LLMs. On the whiteboard, start by sketching a simple downward-sloping curve representing 'Loss' (error) against 'Compute'. The core message here is that model performance is not a mystery or a roll of the dice; it is a predictable power law. We must frame this as a shift from 'trial and error' to 'statistical engineering,' where we can anticipate the quality of a model before we ever flip the switch on a GPU cluster.

Next, we transition to the Kaplan vs. Hoffmann (Chinchilla) debate, which is the most critical conceptual pivot in this lecture. I’ll illustrate this by drawing two sets of coordinates. First, show the 'Kaplan' era intuition which suggested that model size (parameters) was the dominant factor, leading everyone to race toward hundreds of billions of parameters. Then, introduce the 'Chinchilla' correction: for every doubling of model size, we must also double the amount of data. This is the 'equal scaling' rule. I want to highlight the common misconception that bigger is always better; in reality, many early models were 'under-trained' because they had massive brains but were starved of tokens. We will use the '7B parameter model' as our concrete anchor point on the board, calculating that according to Chinchilla (roughly 20 tokens per parameter), we need 140 billion tokens just to be 'optimal.'

To bridge into the practice task, we will walk through the 'Compute-Optimal' frontier. I'll draw a graph with 'Dataset Size' on one axis and 'Model Size' on the other, with an 'Isoloss' curve showing different combinations that achieve the same performance. This visual helps students understand trade-offs. If we double the compute budget, do we just make the model 2x bigger? No—we distribute that extra power across both parameters and data. I will explicitly address the mathematical intuition of 'diminishing returns,' showing how the loss curve flattens out, explaining why it becomes exponentially more expensive to squeeze out the last bits of intelligence.

Finally, we will engage in a 'What-If' exercise to test their grasp of these ratios. I’ll pose a scenario: 'If I have a 7B model and I give it 10x the data recommended by Chinchilla, what happens?' This leads to a discussion on 'over-training,' a strategy used by models like Llama to prioritize inference efficiency over training optimality. This distinction is vital for researchers: Chinchilla tells you how to get the best model for your training dollar, but in the real world, we often spend more on training to make the model smaller and faster for the millions of users who will call the API later. This connects the abstract math of scaling laws to the practical economics of deployment.

tasks: Calculate the optimal number of tokens for a hypothetical 7B parameter model based on Chinchilla scaling ratios.
Predict how loss would change if the compute budget is doubled while keeping parameters constant.

sessions.title: Compute and Cost
sessions.description: This session breaks down the hardware requirements and financial costs associated with training state-of-the-art models. You will learn to estimate FLOPs and translate computational complexity into GPU hours and dollars, providing you with a realistic perspective on the economic barriers and engineering hurdles in the generative AI industry.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Welcome to the session where we peel back the curtain on the brute force of intelligence: the compute and the cold, hard cash required to build these models. To start, we must move away from abstract notions of 'training' and treat LLM development as a massive construction project. I begin by drawing a single 'FLOP' (Floating Point Operation) on the whiteboard—one simple multiplication and addition—and then scale it up to the 'ZettaFLOP' scale. The goal is to make the learner feel the weight of the arithmetic. We explain that training a model is essentially performing billions of these operations per token, across billions of parameters. This leads us to the fundamental 'Rule of Six': for a standard transformer architecture, it takes roughly 6 FLOPs per parameter, per token during the training phase. This mental model is vital because it allows an engineer to sketch the computational cost on a napkin before ever touching a GPU.

Once we have the 'total FLOPs' estimated, I transition the whiteboard sketch to the hardware bottleneck. We move from the math of the model to the reality of the silicon. Here, I introduce the concept of 'Model FLOPs Utilization' (MFU). It's a common trap for beginners to assume that a GPU providing 312 TFLOPS will deliver that full speed; in reality, data movement, overhead, and synchronization across a cluster eat into this efficiency. We discuss why a typical high-end cluster might only achieve 40-50% MFU. By visualizing the data pipeline from memory to the tensor cores, the learner begins to see that 'compute' isn't just a number—it's a physical logistics problem. We then connect this to the dollar sign: if you know your total FLOPs and your expected MFU, you can calculate the total H100-hours required. This transition from 'pure math' to 'budgetary reality' is the core bridge of this session.

Next, we tackle the 'Hidden Costs.' It’s not just about the GPUs; it’s about the interconnects (Infiniband vs. Ethernet) and the failure rates. I like to frame this by asking the class: 'What happens when 1 out of 10,000 GPUs fails mid-training?' This introduces the necessity of checkpointing and the massive engineering overhead of maintaining a stable cluster for months at a time. We also dive into the energy aspect, not just as a cost center, but as a scale comparison. I’ll map the energy used for a model like Llama-3 to the annual energy consumption of an average household. This isn't just for shock value; it helps the student internalize why efficiency (like 4-bit quantization or better architectures) is the primary driver of current research.

To wrap up, we conduct a real-time 'Estimation Challenge.' I provide a hypothetical scenario: a startup wants to train a 10B parameter model on 1 trillion tokens with a $500,000 budget. This exercise forces the learner to apply the 'Rule of Six,' account for MFU, and look up current spot-pricing for cloud compute. The revelation usually hits when they realize that even with half a million dollars, they might fall short if they don't optimize their data or architecture. This practice ensures that the student leaves not just knowing that training is 'expensive,' but knowing exactly how to calculate the price of a model’s soul in both kilowatt-hours and dollars.

tasks: Estimate the cost of training a model given a specific GPU hourly rate and a total FLOP count.
Compare the energy consumption of a large-scale training run to common household energy usage.

sessions.title: Model Size Trade-offs
sessions.description: You will examine the trade-offs between 'hero' models and smaller, more efficient models designed for specific tasks. This session helps you understand the concept of 'emergent properties' in large models versus the deployment efficiency of small models, which is vital for choosing the right architecture for a real-world application.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by drawing a simple spectrum on the board, with 'Efficiency' on one far end and 'Capability' on the other. Explain that in the world of LLMs, we are constantly navigating the tension between 'Hero Models'—the massive, state-of-the-art giants like GPT-4 or Llama-3-70B—and 'Specialized SLMs' (Small Language Models) like Phi-3 or Llama-7B. The core idea is that while bigger is often smarter, it comes with a physical and financial tax that can make it unusable in real-world applications. This sets the stage for a 'fitness for purpose' mindset, moving the student away from the 'bigger is always better' fallacy.

Transition to the concept of Emergent Properties. On the whiteboard, sketch a non-linear graph showing 'Model Size' on the X-axis and 'Accuracy on Complex Task' (like multi-step logic or arithmetic) on the Y-axis. Illustrate how performance stays flat and near-zero for smaller models, then suddenly 'jumps' once a certain parameter threshold is crossed. This is the 'aha' moment for students: explaining that certain behaviors, like chain-of-thought reasoning or zero-shot translation in low-resource languages, aren't just scaled versions of small model features—they are qualitative shifts that only appear in the giants. Use the example of a 3B model failing at a logic puzzle because it lacks the internal 'circuitry' that a 70B model possesses purely by virtue of its scale.

Now, pivot to the reality of deployment by discussing Latency and Throughput. Create a table comparing a 7B and a 70B model. Focus on the 'Time to First Token.' Explain that if a developer is building a real-time coding assistant or a mobile-based chat interface, a 70B model's three-second delay is a dealbreaker, whereas a 7B model's near-instant response feels like magic. Address a common misconception here: learners often think they can just 'optimize' a huge model to be fast, but you must emphasize that memory bandwidth—the physical speed at which data moves from the GPU memory to the processor—is a hard ceiling that favors smaller models.

Introduce a practice moment where students must defend a model choice. Pose the scenario: 'You are building a classification bot that identifies if a customer email is a complaint or a compliment. Do you use the Hero model or the 7B model?' Guide them toward the 7B model. Explain that for narrow, pattern-matching tasks, the 'reasoning' power of a giant is overkill and an expensive waste of compute. This reveals if the student understands that 'smartness' is relative to the task's complexity.

Conclude by discussing the 'Small Model Renaissance.' Explain that with techniques like distillation and high-quality synthetic data, 7B and 8B models are now 'punching above their weight class,' often outperforming older, larger models. The final takeaway for the teacher is to leave the students with the 'Golden Rule of AI Architecture': Use the smallest model that comfortably solves the problem. This prepares them for the practicalities of Unit 4, where they will actually build systems and have to justify their resource consumption.

tasks: Identify three tasks where a 7B model might outperform a 70B model in a production setting due to latency.
Describe one 'emergent property' that typically only appears after a certain parameter threshold is reached.

lectures.title: Alignment
lectures.description: This lecture focuses on the bridge between a 'raw' base model and a helpful assistant, covering the techniques used to make model behavior safe and instruction-following.

sessions.title: Instruction Tuning
sessions.description: You will learn the process of fine-tuning a base model on instruction-response pairs to transform it from a document completer into a conversational agent. Understanding this phase is crucial for seeing how a model learns the 'vibe' and format of human interaction beyond just predicting the next word in a vacuum.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a fundamental misconception many newcomers have: that a 'trained' model is a 'ready-to-use' assistant. I will start by visualizing the Base Model as a 'statistical autocomplete' engine. On the whiteboard, I'll draw a large block representing a pre-trained model and write a simple sentence fragment like 'The capital of France is...' followed by a list of likely continuations. I will explain that while the base model 'knows' the answer is Paris, it doesn't necessarily know that it should answer a direct question. To it, the prompt 'What is the capital of France?' might just as easily be followed by another question in a trivia list, or a header like 'Question 1:'. This transition from a text-completer to a task-follower is the essence of Instruction Tuning.

Next, I will introduce the concept of the 'Instruction-Response Pair' as the primary unit of currency in this phase. On the whiteboard, I'll sketch a table contrasting 'Raw Web Data' (unstructured, noisy, predictive) with 'Instruction Data' (structured, goal-oriented, helpful). The core idea here is that we aren't teaching the model *new* facts; we are teaching it a new *format*—the conversational 'vibe.' I'll emphasize that during this phase, we are narrowing the model's vast probability space to focus on the persona of a helpful AI assistant. This is why it's often called 'Alignment'—we are aligning its output behavior with human expectations.

To make this concrete, I'll walk through the process of 'Instructional Distillation.' We will take a boring, dry paragraph about rain (e.g., a scientific description of precipitation) and demonstrate how to manually carve it into multiple prompts: 'Write a poem about rain,' 'Explain the water cycle to a 5-year-old,' or 'Summarize the causes of rainfall.' This exercise is crucial because it reveals that the underlying knowledge exists within the model parameters already, but needs the right 'instructional key' to be unlocked. I’ll warn the class about the 'lazy model' pitfall, where poor instruction tuning leads to models that repeat the prompt rather than answering it.

Finally, we will contrast the outputs of a Base Model versus an Instruction-Tuned (IT) model. I'll write the prompt 'Write a poem about rain' on the board and simulate the Base Model's likely failure: perhaps it continues with 'and snow' or 'by Robert Frost.' Then, I'll show the IT model's response: an actual poem. This visual comparison highlights the 'Instruction-Following' capability as a distinct skill. I will conclude by explaining that while SFT (Supervised Fine-Tuning) is the technique, 'Instruction Tuning' is the objective, setting the stage for the more technical implementation details of loss functions and data formatting in the next session.

tasks: Convert a raw text paragraph into a set of instruction-completion pairs suitable for fine-tuning.
Explain the difference in output between a base model and an instruction-tuned model for the prompt 'Write a poem about rain'.

sessions.title: Supervised Fine-Tuning
sessions.description: This session dives into the technical implementation of Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), including loss functions and data formatting. You will gain the technical knowledge to structure datasets and evaluate whether an SFT run has successfully captured the desired task-specific style without overfitting to a narrow data distribution.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by transitioning from the conceptual 'vibe' of instruction tuning to the cold, hard mechanics of Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). The core idea to impress upon the students is that SFT is essentially 'Next Token Prediction' but with a mask. On the whiteboard, draw the structure of a training example: a System Prompt, a User Query, and the Assistant Response. Explain that during SFT, the model processes the entire sequence, but we only calculate loss—and thus only 'punish' or 'reward' the model—on the tokens belonging to the Assistant's response. This is a crucial distinction; if we calculated loss on the user's prompt, the model would try to memorize how users ask questions rather than how to answer them. This 'Loss Masking' is the technical lever that turns a general-purpose model into a specialized tool.

Now, let's look at the mathematical engine: Cross-Entropy Loss. Visualize a probability distribution over the entire vocabulary for a single token slot. In SFT, we have a 'ground truth'—the actual token used by the human labeler in our dataset. The Cross-Entropy loss is the penalty for every bit of probability mass the model assigns to any token *other* than that ground truth token. Use the whiteboard to show a simplified calculation: if the model is 20% sure the next word is 'Paris' but the label says 'London', the loss function forces the gradients to shift the model’s internal weights to make 'London' more probable next time. Explain that the goal of SFT is to minimize this total loss across thousands of high-quality examples until the model's internal distribution mirrors the distribution of the training data.

At this stage, students often fall into the trap of thinking 'more data is always better.' We must counter this by discussing the 'Garbage In, Garbage Out' reality of SFT. Use a whiteboard diagram to illustrate a 'Narrow Distribution' vs. a 'Diverse Distribution.' If your SFT data consists of 1,000 examples that all start with 'I am happy to help you with that,' the model will suffer from 'mode collapse'—it will become a repetitive sycophant that lacks the flexibility to handle nuanced prompts. The most important lesson here is that 1,000 diverse, perfectly labeled examples are worth more than 100,000 noisy, scraped examples. Introduce the 'Curse of Quality': if the training labels contain factual errors or formatting inconsistencies, the model will faithfully learn those errors as the 'correct' way to behave.

To wrap up, we pivot to a diagnostic exercise. Ask the students to imagine they are training a model to write code, but the loss isn't going down. We use this to walk through the common pitfalls: lack of variety, poor labeling, and formatting leaks (where the model learns the specific metadata of the dataset rather than the logic). This exercise is designed to shift their mindset from 'training a model' to 'curating an experience.' The teacher should emphasize that SFT is not about teaching the model new facts—it already 'knows' things from pre-training—it’s about teaching the model which 'drawer' of its memory to open when it sees a specific type of user request.

tasks: Define the Cross-Entropy loss used during a standard SFT training step.
List three common pitfalls in SFT data collection, such as lack of variety or poor labeling.

sessions.title: RLHF and Preference Learning
sessions.description: You will explore Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF), specifically how reward models are trained on human preferences to guide the LLM's policy. This session provides the conceptual framework for advanced alignment techniques like PPO and DPO, which are the industry standard for creating 'helpful, honest, and harmless' AI.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing the limitation of Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT). While SFT is excellent at teaching a model the 'vibe' of a response, it struggles with ambiguity. If you ask a model to 'Write a funny joke,' there isn't one single 'correct' answer that a loss function can easily converge on. On the whiteboard, I will draw a branching path of possible model responses to a single prompt, illustrating that while multiple paths are 'good,' some are slightly better than others. This sets the stage for Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) as a way to move beyond binary 'right vs. wrong' labels and into the realm of 'better vs. worse.'

Next, I introduce the three-stage architecture of RLHF: the Policy Model, the Reward Model, and the Optimization loop. I will draw a central diagram showing a human labeler presented with two different outputs for the same prompt. The labeler chooses the preferred one. The key insight here is that humans find it much easier to rank items than to generate perfect examples from scratch. This preference data is then used to train the 'Reward Model'—a separate neural network that acts as a mathematical proxy for human taste. I'll emphasize that this Reward Model is essentially a 'critic' that learns to assign a high score to things humans like and a low score to things they don't.

Then, we transition to the actual learning phase where the Reward Model trains the Policy Model (the LLM itself). On the board, I will visualize this as a feedback loop. The LLM generates a response, the Reward Model 'grades' it, and that grade is used as a signal to update the LLM’s weights. A critical concept to introduce here is 'KL Divergence' as a safety anchor. I'll explain that without this anchor, the model might try to 'hack' the reward model by generating gibberish that the reward model happens to like—a phenomenon known as Reward Hacking. I’ll use the analogy of a student learning to guess what the teacher wants to hear rather than actually learning the material.

To solidify this, we will engage in a 'Human Reward' exercise. I'll present the class with two model responses to a complex ethical query and ask them to rank them. This exercise is designed to reveal the subjectivity of 'goodness' and demonstrate why collecting diverse human feedback is the most expensive and difficult part of the process. This naturally leads to a brief mention of Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), where I explain that we can now skip the separate Reward Model and optimize the LLM directly on the preference pairs, simplifying the pipeline significantly.

Finally, I will wrap up by connecting RLHF back to the 'Helpful, Honest, and Harmless' (HHH) framework. I’ll explain that RLHF is the specific tool used to 'dial in' the model's personality and safety boundaries. We conclude by acknowledging that while RLHF makes models incredibly steerable, it also introduces the risk of 'sycophancy,' where the model agrees with the user just to get a high reward. This sets the stage for our next session on safety guardrails and the inevitable tension between being helpful and being safe.

tasks: Sketch the feedback loop between the human labeler, the reward model, and the policy model.
Explain why supervised learning alone is often insufficient for capturing complex human preferences.

sessions.title: Guardrails and Refusals
sessions.description: In this session, you will learn how models are trained to refuse harmful or toxic requests through safety alignment. Understanding the mechanism of refusals helps you differentiate between a model's 'knowledge' and its 'behavioral constraints,' which is essential for both building safe systems and debugging unintentional refusals.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this final session of the Alignment lecture by drawing a clear, visual distinction on the board between a model's 'Internal Knowledge Graph' and its 'Behavioral Filter.' Up until now, students might assume that if a model refuses to answer a question, it simply doesn't 'know' the answer. We must debunk this immediately. Use the analogy of a professional librarian who knows exactly where the 'Anarchist Cookbook' is located but is strictly forbidden by policy from handing it to a minor. This distinction is the bedrock of understanding safety alignment; we are not deleting data from the model's brain, we are training a secondary 'refusal reflex' that triggers when specific semantic patterns are detected.

To visualize the mechanism of refusals, draw a simplified decision flow. Start with a user query like 'How do I build a dangerous device?' entering the transformer. Explain that during the Safety Fine-Tuning phase (often a subset of RLHF), the model is explicitly trained on 'negative examples.' Instead of the standard SFT goal of 'predict the next token correctly,' the goal here is to steer the probability distribution toward a specific 'Refusal Cluster.' On the whiteboard, illustrate this as a vector space where certain topics—violence, self-harm, hate speech—have been mapped to a high-probability exit ramp leading to phrases like 'I cannot fulfill this request.' It is vital to emphasize that this is a learned behavior, not a hard-coded keyword filter, which explains why models can sometimes be 'jailbroken' by changing the context (the 'Grandma' exploit).

Next, we tackle the 'Tension of Objectives.' On one side of the board, write 'Helpfulness' and on the other, 'Harmlessness.' Explain that these two goals are often in direct competition. If a safety policy is too aggressive, the model becomes 'over-refining'—refusing to write a murder mystery novel because it contains 'violence.' This is a common pitfall in production models. We want the students to understand that 'Alignment' is a delicate balancing act of loss functions. If we penalize the model too heavily for any proximity to a sensitive topic, we destroy its utility. This leads into the first practice task: present the students with a hypothetical refusal where a model refuses to explain the history of the French Revolution because it involved 'guillotines.' Ask the students to identify if this is a failure of the safety policy or an over-correction, and how the prompt might be adjusted to bypass this while staying safe.

We conclude by discussing 'Guardrails' as a system-level architecture rather than just a model-level behavior. Move from the internal weights of the LLM to the external 'wrapper.' Sketch a diagram showing the 'Input Guardrail' (checking the prompt before it hits the LLM) and the 'Output Guardrail' (checking the response before the user sees it). This illustrates that in a production environment, safety is a multi-layered defense. The most important takeaway is that while 'Refusals' are trained into the model's weights to handle nuance, 'Guardrails' are often deterministic filters used to provide a final safety net. This distinction prepares students for the final unit of the course, where they will build their own evaluation and safety suites for production-grade agents.

tasks: Analyze a refusal response from an LLM and identify the likely safety policy it is enforcing.
Discuss the tension between model helpfulness and model safety.

lectures.title: Efficient Adaptation
lectures.description: This lecture introduces the practical techniques used to adapt massive models to specific tasks without the prohibitive cost of full-parameter updates.

sessions.title: Full Fine-Tuning vs Adapters
sessions.description: You will compare the computational costs and storage requirements of updating every weight in a model versus using modular 'adapter' layers. This comparison will help you decide when the extra performance of full fine-tuning is worth the massive infrastructure overhead compared to lightweight alternatives.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by framing the problem as one of logistics and physics. We've spent the previous units learning how models work, but now we must confront the reality of their size. Draw a massive, solid block on the whiteboard labeled '70 Billion Parameters'. Explain that in Full Fine-Tuning, we treat this block as a single, clay-like entity where every single parameter can be reshaped. The core idea to emphasize is that while this gives us the most 'degrees of freedom' to teach the model new things, it requires the gradient of every single parameter to be stored in GPU memory during training. Most learners underestimate the hardware jump from inference to training; point out that if the model takes 140GB of VRAM just to sit there, full fine-tuning will require many times that, often demanding an expensive H100 cluster for even modest tasks.

Transition to the storage and deployment nightmare. Draw ten more identical 140GB blocks next to the first one. This visual represents a company trying to maintain ten different versions of a model—one for customer support, one for coding, one for creative writing, etc. The instructor should pause here to let the math sink in: we are talking about terabytes of storage for what are essentially minor behavioral variations. This leads naturally into the concept of 'Adapters.' Draw a tiny, modular box next to the massive 70B block. Explain that instead of rewriting the entire book, we are essentially adding a few sticky notes between the pages. The weights of the 70B model are 'frozen' (draw a lock icon), and we only train the tiny new layers. This isn't just about saving money; it's about making AI manageable for teams without massive infrastructure.

Now, address the psychological aspect of the model: Catastrophic Forgetting. Use the analogy of a student who learns medical terminology so intensely that they forget how to speak casual English. In Full Fine-Tuning, because every weight is updated, the 'gradient descent' might inadvertently overwrite the general-purpose reasoning capabilities the model gained during pre-training. By contrast, Adapters act as a safety buffer. Because the original weights are never touched, the base intelligence of the model remains pristine, and the adapter simply acts as a 'filter' or 'translator' for the specific task at hand. This distinction is vital for production systems where you cannot afford for a specialized model to lose its basic sanity or safety guardrails.

Engage the learners with a quick mental calculation exercise. Ask them to compare storing 10 versions of a 70B model (Full Fine-Tuning) versus 10 adapters that are 0.1% the size. The goal of this exercise is to shift their mindset from 'how do I get the highest benchmark score' to 'how do I build a sustainable system.' A common misconception is that adapters are always inferior; the instructor should clarify that for many domain-specific tasks, the performance difference is negligible, but the operational difference is the difference between a project being feasible or impossible. Close by showing how these adapters can be 'hot-swapped' on a single server, allowing one base model to serve many different specialized functions simultaneously.

tasks: Calculate the storage space required for 10 full fine-tuned checkpoints of a 70B model versus 10 adapter modules.
Explain the 'catastrophic forgetting' problem associated with full fine-tuning.

sessions.title: LoRA and Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning
sessions.description: This session teaches you the Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) method, which approximates weight changes using low-rank matrices. You will learn the linear algebra behind LoRA and why it allows developers to fine-tune massive models on consumer hardware, democratizing the ability to build custom LLMs.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing the elephant in the room: the sheer impossibility of training modern LLMs on standard hardware. If a 70B parameter model requires gigabytes of memory just to load, computing gradients for every single weight is a non-starter for most organizations. Introduce the concept of 'Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning' (PEFT) as a paradigm shift—instead of trying to move the whole mountain, we identify the small, high-leverage points that can steer the model’s behavior. The core intuition to establish is that while a model has billions of weights, the 'intrinsic dimension' of a specific task (like learning to output JSON) is actually quite small. 

Transition to the visual 'Whiteboard' centerpiece of this session: the decomposition of a weight update. On the board, draw a massive square matrix representing the original weight 'W'. Explain that in traditional fine-tuning, we calculate a change matrix 'delta W' of the same size. Then, introduce the LoRA breakthrough: we can approximate 'delta W' by multiplying two much thinner, rectangular matrices, A and B. Draw these as a tall skinny rectangle and a short wide rectangle. The key realization for the learner here is the 'rank' r—explain that by choosing a small r (like 8 or 16), we are forcing the model to find the most efficient path to change its behavior, effectively ignoring the noise and focusing on the signal.

Now, dive into the linear algebra mechanics that make this work. Explain that during training, the original weights 'W' are frozen—literally locked in stone—so no gradients are calculated for them. Only matrices A and B are updated. This is where you address the first practice task: demonstrate that if 'W' is 4096 by 4096, but 'r' is only 8, we reduce the trainable parameters from roughly 16 million down to about 65,000. This visualization is crucial because it transforms 'efficiency' from an abstract concept into a hard mathematical reality. A common misconception to head off here is that a lower rank always means worse performance; explain that if the rank is too high, the model might overfit to the training data, while if it's too low, it won't have enough capacity to learn the new task.

Move the discussion to the inference phase and the 'No-Latency' promise of LoRA. This addresses the second practice task. On the whiteboard, show the equation for the model's output: h = Wx + (BA)x. Use a different color to show that because of the distributive property, we can mathematically combine these back into a single matrix: W_new = W + BA. Explain the 'merging' process—how a developer can take the small LoRA adapter weights, add them back to the base model, and ship a single model file that has zero extra computational cost during use. This is the 'holy grail' of deployment: the agility of a custom model with the speed of the original.

Conclude by framing LoRA as the 'democratization' of AI. Because we only need to store and tune these tiny A and B matrices, a single GPU that previously could only run a model can now be used to train it. The final takeaway should be that LoRA isn't just a compression trick; it’s a strategic choice to focus a model’s learning capacity on exactly what matters for the target application.

tasks: Describe how the rank 'r' in LoRA affects the number of trainable parameters.
Explain how a LoRA adapter can be merged back into the base model weights for inference.

sessions.title: Quantization
sessions.description: You will learn how to reduce the precision of model weights (e.g., from 16-bit to 4-bit) to save memory and increase speed. This session covers techniques like AWQ and bitsandbytes, giving you the tools to run powerful models on local devices or reduce your cloud serving costs significantly.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by framing the physical constraints of Large Language Models. A model with 7 billion parameters is often touted as 'small,' but when stored in standard FP16 (half-precision), it requires 14GB of VRAM just to load the weights. This creates a hard ceiling for most consumer GPUs and significantly inflates cloud inference costs. The core goal of this session is to introduce quantization not just as a compression trick, but as a fundamental shift in how we represent numbers to squeeze massive intelligence into limited hardware.

Begin the whiteboard session by visualizing the number line. Contrast high-precision floating points (FP32/FP16) with discrete integers (INT8/INT4). Explain the concept of 'mapping' or 'scaling factors': how we can take a range of continuous weights and snap them to the nearest available discrete bucket. It is crucial to emphasize that quantization is a lossy process. The teacher should draw a normal distribution representing model weights—noting that most weights cluster near zero—and show how 'outliers' (very large or small values) pose a challenge, as they force the 'buckets' to be spread too thin, leading to rounding errors in the more frequent central values.

Transition into the practical math of VRAM calculation. Walk through the calculation: (Number of Parameters) * (Bits per Parameter / 8) = Bytes. For a 7B model, 16-bit (2 bytes) equals 14GB; 8-bit (1 byte) equals 7GB; 4-bit (0.5 bytes) equals 3.5GB. This visual breakdown immediately demonstrates why 4-bit quantization is the 'golden ratio' for local deployment, as it allows a 7B model to fit comfortably on an 8GB laptop GPU with room left for the KV cache. To prevent the misconception that memory is the only factor, explain that while memory footprint drops, the CPU/GPU must often 'dequantize' these numbers back to FP16 for actual computation, meaning the speedup comes from reduced data transfer (I/O) rather than simpler math.

Introduce the modern ecosystem of tools, specifically 'bitsandbytes' for on-the-fly quantization during training (QLoRA) and 'AWQ' (Activation-aware Weight Quantization) for deployment. Explain the 'Activation-aware' logic: not all weights are created equal. Some weights (the 1% 'salient' weights) are much more important for model performance than others. AWQ works by protecting these important weights while aggressively compressing the rest. This explains why we can go down to 4-bit with negligible hits to perplexity.

Conclude with a discussion on 'Perplexity' as the diagnostic metric for quantization health. Pose a scenario to the class: if we quantize a model and its perplexity spikes, what does that mean for the user? The answer is a loss of nuance and reasoning capability. Use this to bridge to the practice task, asking students to debate the trade-off: is a 70B model quantized to 4-bit (35GB) better or worse than a 7B model at 16-bit (14GB)? This forces them to realize that 'bigger model + more compression' often outperforms 'smaller model + less compression,' which is the fundamental logic driving the current local LLM movement.

tasks: Calculate the VRAM required to load a 7B model in 16-bit, 8-bit, and 4-bit precision.
Discuss the typical impact of quantization on a model's perplexity.

sessions.title: Prompting vs RAG vs Fine-Tuning
sessions.description: In this synthesis session, you will develop a decision framework for when to use prompting, when to implement RAG, and when to fine-tune. This session is critical for your goal of application development, ensuring you don't spend weeks fine-tuning a model for a problem that could have been solved with a better prompt or a simple vector search.
sessions.sessionOutline:
This session serves as the critical 'Grand Synthesis' for Unit 3. Up to this point, learners have been deep in the weeds of LoRA, quantization, and fine-tuning mechanics. The teacher must now zoom out to address the single most common engineering mistake in the LLM era: choosing the most complex tool (fine-tuning) for a problem that requires a simpler one (prompting or RAG). To set the stage, the teacher should draw a three-way spectrum on the whiteboard. On the left is 'Prompting' (high speed, zero weight updates), in the middle is 'RAG' (dynamic external memory), and on the right is 'Fine-Tuning' (permanent internal knowledge update). The central goal is to teach students how to navigate this trade-off between the 'Static Brain' of training and the 'Dynamic Context' of inference.

Begin the first beat by defining the boundaries of 'Context Window' vs. 'Model Weights.' Explain that prompting and RAG are effectively providing 'open-book' materials to the model at query time, whereas fine-tuning is 'studying' to internalize behavior. The key insight here is that LLMs are notorious for being poor at memorizing precise facts via fine-tuning (hallucinations often increase), but they are excellent at learning patterns, style, and formatting. The teacher should illustrate this by comparing a doctor reading a new patient file (RAG) versus a student attending medical school to learn how to speak like a doctor (Fine-Tuning). This clarifies that if the data changes daily—like stock prices or news—fine-tuning is a waste of resources because the model will be 'out of date' the moment training finishes.

Next, introduce the 'RAG vs. Fine-Tuning' decision matrix. Use the whiteboard to plot two axes: 'Need for External Data' and 'Need for Specialized Behavior.' A common misconception learners have is that fine-tuning helps a model 'know' more. The teacher must correct this by explaining that RAG is for truth and retrieval, while Fine-Tuning is for form and vocabulary. If a company has 10,000 PDFs of technical manuals, they need RAG to find the right page. If that company needs the model to strictly output valid JSON in a very specific proprietary schema that it keeps failing at, they need Fine-Tuning. This leads into the first practice task: evaluating scenarios like domain-specific jargon (Fine-Tuning/Prompting) vs. real-time news (RAG).

Transition into the 'Cost-Benefit' beat, which is essential for the application development focus. The teacher should draw a simple table comparing latency, storage, and maintenance. Fine-tuning requires managing model versions and deployment overhead; RAG requires managing a vector database and retrieval pipelines. The teacher should warn about 'catastrophic forgetting' in fine-tuning—where the model gets so good at one task it loses its general reasoning—and compare it to the 'context window bloat' in RAG, where too much retrieved info makes the model confused. This sets up the second practice task: building a strategy for a customer support bot. The instructor should guide students to see that a hybrid approach is often best—using RAG for the help-center articles and a small LoRA adapter to ensure the bot maintains a specific brand voice.

Conclude by reinforcing the 'Hierarchy of Effort.' Start with a prompt. If that fails, try few-shot examples. If the context is too large, build a RAG system. Only when the model fundamentally cannot follow the 'style' or 'logic' of the task after these steps should the engineer reach for the fine-tuning tools discussed earlier in the lecture. This leaves the student not just with the technical skill of how to tune a model, but the professional wisdom of when to avoid it.

tasks: Given three scenarios—domain-specific jargon, real-time news access, and style replication—assign the best adaptation strategy to each.
Create a cost-benefit matrix comparing RAG and Fine-Tuning for a customer support use case.

projects.stage_description: Apply Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) using LoRA to adapt a base LLM to recognize and extract structured metadata from scientific literature.
projects.deliverable_increment: A trained LoRA adapter weight set and a configuration file for loading the specialized model backbone.

exams.title: Training and Adaptation Certification Exam
exams.goal: Verify the learner's ability to select and implement the correct model adaptation strategy based on compute constraints, data availability, and performance goals.
sections: Comprehensive evaluation of pretraining scaling laws, alignment techniques (SFT/RLHF), and efficient fine-tuning methods (LoRA/Quantization).

Select the appropriate PEFT method for a resource-constrained environment.
