units.title: Building with LLMs
units.description: Shift from model development to system orchestration by mastering advanced prompt engineering, RAG pipelines, and the design of autonomous agents.

lectures.title: Prompting
lectures.description: This lecture transitions from black-box API interactions to engineering high-precision instructions, focusing on how specific input structures and reasoning patterns unlock complex model behaviors.

sessions.title: Prompt Structure
sessions.description: This session teaches you the anatomy of a professional prompt, including personas, task delimiters, and constraints. You will learn to eliminate ambiguity in model instructions, ensuring that your LLM applications behave predictably across different inputs. Mastering these building blocks is essential for achieving the conceptual mastery and reliability required for production-level AI development.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by challenging the common misconception that an LLM is a 'human-like' entity that can intuit our hidden needs. Instead, visualize the model as a statistical completion engine that is highly sensitive to the initial conditions we set. The primary goal of this session is to move the learner from 'chatting' with AI to 'engineering' its inputs. Use the analogy of a director giving instructions to an actor: if the director is vague, the performance will be inconsistent. To fix this, we introduce the concept of 'Anatomy of a Prompt'—a structured framework that transforms a fuzzy request into a precise command.

On the whiteboard, sketch out the four pillars of a high-performance prompt: Persona, Context, Task, and Constraints. Begin with the 'Persona.' Explain that by assigning a role like 'Senior Security Engineer' or 'Creative Marketing Assistant,' we are effectively narrowing the model's probability space toward specific professional vocabularies and styles. This isn't just flavor text; it serves as a high-level filter for the latent knowledge the model retrieves. If a student asks why they can't just ask the question directly, explain that without a persona, the model often defaults to a generic, 'safe' assistant tone that lacks the necessary depth for specialized tasks.

Next, introduce the 'Task' and 'Context,' but focus heavily on the use of 'Delimiters' to separate them. This is a critical technical pivot. Use the whiteboard to show how characters like triple backticks (```), XML tags (<text></text>), or dashes (---) act as structural anchors. Explain that delimiters prevent 'Instruction Injection,' where the model might confuse the data it's processing with the instructions it's following. For example, if you ask a model to summarize a document that contains the phrase 'stop summarizing and tell a joke,' the model might fail without clear delimiters. This visual separation is the most important idea for ensuring reliability in production-grade software where inputs are dynamic.

Transition into 'Constraints' and 'Output Indicators.' Constraints define the 'No-Go' zones—word counts, forbidden phrases, or specific formatting rules. On the board, contrast a 'Negative Constraint' (Don't do X) with a 'Positive Constraint' (Always do Y). Emphasize that LLMs often struggle with negative constraints; it is usually more effective to tell the model exactly what to include rather than what to omit. Follow this with 'Output Indicators,' showing how starting the response with a specific word or tag (e.g., 'Summary:') forces the model into the right completion path from the very first token. This reduces the 'drifting' effect where a model starts a response with irrelevant preamble.

Conclude by leading a walkthrough of a 'broken' prompt. Present a vague, one-sentence instruction and ask the class to identify where the ambiguity lies. Use the practice session to have them refactor this prompt using the components discussed—adding a persona, wrapping the source text in XML tags, and defining a strict output format. The goal of this exercise is to reveal that prompt variance is usually a failure of the engineer to define boundaries, not a failure of the model's intelligence. This sets the foundation for the entire unit: that language, when structured correctly, becomes a reliable programming interface.

tasks: Identify the instruction, context, and output indicator in a provided complex prompt.
Refactor a vague prompt using delimiters and clear persona assignments to reduce output variance.

sessions.title: Few-Shot Examples
sessions.description: This session explores the mechanics of in-context learning through the strategic use of demonstrations. You will understand how the number, order, and relevance of examples influence the model's pattern-matching capabilities. This technique allows you to steer model behavior without fine-tuning, providing a fast and cost-effective way to handle niche or proprietary formats.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by framing 'In-Context Learning' (ICL) as the model's superpower: the ability to learn a new task without shifting a single weight in its neural network. Start by sketching a simple input box on the whiteboard. Explain that while zero-shot prompting relies on the model's pre-trained internal 'average' of a concept, providing examples—Few-Shot prompting—actually reshapes the probability distribution of the next token in real-time. Use the metaphor of a 'tuning fork': the examples provide the pitch, and the model resonates to match it. This is a critical transition from 'asking' the model to do something to 'showing' the model how to do it.

Draw a horizontal line representing the prompt and divide it into 'Demonstrations' and 'Query'. Use a sentiment analysis example to illustrate why this matters. If you ask a model to label sentiment as 'Positive' or 'Negative', it might give you a sentence explaining why. But if you provide three examples like 'Text: I love this. Label: POS', the model instantly recognizes the pattern requirement. Emphasize that the model isn't just learning the labels; it is learning the syntax, the brevity, and the specific formatting you desire. This is where you address a common misconception: learners often think they need hundreds of examples. In reality, the 'Goldilocks zone' is often between 3 and 8 examples; beyond that, you hit diminishing returns or context window limits.

Next, visualize the 'Example Selection' strategy on the board. Not all examples are created equal. Explain the 'Recency Bias'—the tendency of models to over-weight the final example provided before the query. Illustrate this by showing how a model might start repeating the label of the last example if the prompt is poorly balanced. Introduce the idea of 'Diversity and Relevance.' If the user's query is about a broken toaster, providing three examples of happy restaurant reviews is less effective than one example of a technical hardware complaint. The logic here is that the model uses the examples to retrieve the relevant 'latent space' of knowledge; the closer the examples are to the target task, the more accurate the mapping.

Transition to the 'Label Distribution' problem. This is a subtle but frequent source of error in production. If you provide five examples where the sentiment is always 'Positive' and then ask the model to evaluate a 'Negative' text, the model is statistically biased toward the majority label it just saw. Teach the instructors to advise students to always balance their labels. Use a small exercise here: ask the students to draft a 3-shot prompt for classifying fruit ripeness. If they use three 'Ripe' examples, point out that the model will likely never dare to call a fruit 'Unripe' because the pattern suggests a constant output.

Finally, discuss the 'Format-Logic' bridge. Few-shot isn't just for classification; it’s for complex data transformation. Show a whiteboard example of converting a messy address string into a clean JSON object. By providing examples of how to handle edge cases—like a missing zip code or an apartment number—you are essentially 'programming' the model's edge-case logic through demonstration. This session concludes by reinforcing that Few-Shot is the fastest way to prototype. If Few-Shot fails to capture the nuance, only then should a developer consider the much higher cost of fine-tuning.

tasks: Compare model performance on a sentiment analysis task using zero-shot vs. few-shot prompting.
Determine the optimal number of examples for a specific data transformation task through iterative testing.

sessions.title: Reasoning Prompts
sessions.description: This session introduces techniques like Chain-of-Thought (CoT) and Least-to-Most prompting to enhance the model's logical deduction. You will learn how to prompt the model to 'think step-by-step' to solve multi-step math or logic problems. These patterns are critical for building reliable applications where the 'how' of the answer is as important as the 'what'.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing a fundamental limitation of Large Language Models: their tendency to 'rush' to an answer. On the whiteboard, draw a simple box representing the Transformer model. Show an input (the prompt) and an immediate output (the answer). Explain that for complex logic, the model often fails because it attempts to compute the entire solution in a single forward pass—essentially trying to do multi-step mental math in a blink. The core concept here is that computational depth in LLMs is tied to the number of tokens generated. To solve harder problems, we must force the model to 'think' by externalizing its reasoning into the context window.

Introduce the 'Chain-of-Thought' (CoT) technique not just as a magic phrase like 'Let's think step-by-step,' but as a structural bridge. Use the whiteboard to contrast a standard prompt (Q -> A) with a CoT prompt (Q -> Reasoning Steps -> A). Explain that by generating reasoning tokens first, the model uses its own previous outputs as a 'working memory' to inform the final answer. This is the most important takeaway: the model's accuracy on logic tasks is proportional to the transparency and granularity of its intermediate steps.

Moving to more complex scenarios, introduce 'Least-to-Most' prompting as a strategy for decomposition. On the board, visualize a large, intimidating word problem being broken down into a tree of smaller, manageable sub-questions. Explain that while CoT is linear, Least-to-Most is hierarchical. This prevents the model from getting lost in a 'hallucination spiral' where one small error at the start of a long chain of thought ruins the entire result. By solving sub-problems sequentially, we provide a more stable foundation for the final conclusion.

To bridge into practice, introduce a word problem involving multiple variables—something like a logic puzzle or a multi-step math equation. Ask the students to observe how a zero-shot model might confidently provide the wrong number. Then, guide them through implementing a CoT prompt. The goal of this exercise is for students to see the 'flip' in model behavior. They should notice that when the model is forced to explain its logic, it often catches its own potential errors before reaching the final line.

Finally, we tackle the concept of 'Self-Consistency' as a reliability layer. Draw three parallel chains of thought on the whiteboard leading to different (or identical) answers. Explain that LLMs are probabilistic; a single chain of thought might hit a 'bad' token path. By sampling multiple reasoning paths and taking a majority vote on the final answer, we significantly boost performance on math and symbolic reasoning tasks. Warn students about the cost-accuracy trade-off here: more reasoning paths mean more tokens and higher latency, which is the primary hurdle in moving these advanced prompting techniques into production environments.

tasks: Implement a Chain-of-Thought prompt for a word problem that a standard prompt fails to solve.
Analyze how self-consistency checks can improve the accuracy of reasoning-heavy outputs.

sessions.title: Structured Output and Reliability
sessions.description: This session covers how to force LLMs to return valid JSON, YAML, or XML formats for programmatic consumption. You will learn to use schema definitions and validation loops to bridge the gap between natural language and traditional software code. This is a foundational step for any developer aiming to integrate LLMs into larger technical stacks.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by addressing the 'Chasm of Unpredictability'—the gap between the fluid, natural language generated by LLMs and the rigid, deterministic schemas required by software engineering. For any AI application to move beyond a chatbot and into a production system, it must speak the language of code: JSON, YAML, or XML. I’ll start on the whiteboard by drawing a simple API pipeline, showing how a stray sentence like 'Here is your data:' appearing before a JSON block can crash a downstream database script. The goal here is to shift the learner's mindset from 'asking' the model for information to 'constraining' the model into a data structure.

To bridge this gap, I will introduce the concept of the Schema-First Prompt. Instead of simply saying 'Give me a JSON of this user profile,' we will visualize a structured template on the board that explicitly defines keys and expected data types. I will explain why including an example of the desired empty schema within the prompt provides the model with a structural 'skeleton' to fill. A key pedagogical point here is the 'Instruction Placement'—placing the structural constraints at the end of the prompt to take advantage of the model's recency bias, ensuring the very first token it generates is the opening brace of our JSON object.

Next, we will tackle the most common failure modes: the 'Preamble' and the 'Markdown Wrap.' Learners often struggle when a model helpfully adds 'Sure, here is your JSON:' at the beginning. I will demonstrate 'Few-Shot Structural Steering,' where we provide one or two examples where the input is a paragraph and the output starts immediately with the data structure. This visual on the board will help students understand that we are training the model’s 'next-token prediction' to favor syntax over conversational filler. We’ll also discuss why using the 'System Message' for schema definition is more robust than the 'User Message' in many model architectures.

For the first practice moment, we will look at a messy paragraph about a fictional company and attempt to extract entities. I’ll ask students to write a prompt that fails first—usually by being too vague—and then show them how to use delimiters like 'Output Format: [JSON ONLY]' to tighten the constraints. We will intentionally look for a 'trailing comma' error, which frequently breaks standard parsers, and discuss how to prompt specifically to avoid these syntax hallucinations. This exercise reveals the fragility of language-to-code translation and why validation is not optional.

Finally, I will introduce the concept of the Validation Loop. On the whiteboard, I’ll diagram a simple recursive logic: the LLM generates a response, a Python `json.loads()` attempt is made, and if it fails, the error message itself is fed back into the LLM with the original prompt for self-correction. This 'Programmatic Correctness' loop is the hallmark of a professional AI engineer. We will conclude by emphasizing that while prompting for structure is powerful, the ultimate reliability comes from combining specific prompt engineering with robust error-handling code in the application layer.

tasks: Create a prompt that extracts entity information from a paragraph into a strictly valid JSON schema.
Debug a model output that breaks a JSON parser by adjusting the prompt constraints.

lectures.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation
lectures.description: This lecture addresses the 'knowledge cutoff' and hallucination problems by teaching you how to connect LLMs to external, private data sources via vector search.

sessions.title: Why Retrieval
sessions.description: This session defines the RAG architecture and why it is often superior to fine-tuning for knowledge-heavy tasks. You will grasp the conceptual difference between the model's internal weights (parametric memory) and external databases (non-parametric memory). This provides the framework for deciding when to use retrieval to ensure your application remains factual and up-to-date.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by framing the core tension in modern LLM development: the 'Brain vs. Library' dilemma. Explain that while an LLM feels like it knows everything, its knowledge is frozen in time at the moment training ended. Use the whiteboard to draw a line between 'Parametric Memory' (the weights, representing patterns and logic) and 'Non-parametric Memory' (external data, representing facts). The central insight for the student is that an LLM should be treated more like a reasoning engine and less like a database. If the model relies only on its weights, it is prone to hallucination because it prioritizes linguistic plausibility over factual accuracy.

Introduce the concept of 'Knowledge Cutoff' through a concrete scenario, such as asking a model about a news event that happened this morning. This leads naturally into the RAG architecture. Contrast this with the Fine-Tuning approach. On the whiteboard, illustrate Fine-Tuning as 're-training the brain'—a slow, expensive process that is good for learning style or specific jargon but poor for memorizing rapidly changing facts. In contrast, RAG is like giving the model an 'open-book exam.' By providing the model with a relevant document snippet at the time of the query, we offload the burden of memory to an external system, which is cheaper to update and easier to verify.

Now, walk through the basic data flow on the whiteboard to demystify the 'magic' for the learner. Draw a flow starting from the User Query, hitting a Search Engine or Database first, and then feeding both the Query and the retrieved Context into the LLM. Emphasize that the LLM's role here is to synthesize the provided context, not to recall it from its own memory. This distinction is vital because it introduces the concept of grounding: the model can now cite its sources, which provides a level of interpretability that raw model generation lacks.

Address a common misconception: that RAG and Fine-Tuning are mutually exclusive. Explain that they solve different problems—Fine-Tuning is for form, while RAG is for facts. To solidify this, pivot to the practice task. Ask the students to consider a medical diagnostic tool: do we fine-tune it on patient records, or do we use RAG? The goal of the exercise is for them to realize that fine-tuning on sensitive, evolving patient data is a security and accuracy nightmare, whereas RAG allows for real-time updates and strict access control. End the session by showing that RAG isn't just about 'knowing more'; it’s about making the model more reliable by providing a 'source of truth' it is forced to respect.

tasks: Contrast a scenario where fine-tuning is appropriate with one where RAG is a better technical choice.
Diagram the data flow of a basic RAG request from user query to final answer.

sessions.title: Chunking and Embedding Documents
sessions.description: This session focuses on the data preparation pipeline, teaching you how to split large documents into meaningful 'chunks' and convert them into vectors. You will learn how chunk size and overlap strategies impact the model's ability to find relevant context. Proper preprocessing is the most significant factor in RAG performance, making this a vital skill for application developers.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start by illustrating the concept of the 'Context Window' as a physical container. Explain that while our previous session established that we need external data, we cannot simply pour an entire 500-page manual into an LLM because it would overflow the token limit or, even if it fit, lead to the 'lost in the middle' phenomenon where the model ignores critical details. This sets the stage for 'Chunking'—the art of breaking a monolithic document into bite-sized, digestible pieces that the model can actually use.

Visualize the document as a long ribbon being cut into segments. Introduce 'Fixed-size Chunking' first. Draw a simple sequence of characters and show a vertical cut every 'n' characters. Use this to highlight the immediate problem: if we cut mid-sentence, we lose the context. For example, if 'The password is 12345' is split between two chunks, neither chunk knows the full secret. This naturally leads into the concept of 'Overlap'. Demonstrate on the whiteboard how sliding the window back a few tokens for each new chunk creates a 'contextual bridge,' ensuring that semantic meaning isn't severed at the boundaries.

Move the discussion from character-based splitting to 'Recursive Character Splitting' and 'Semantic Chunking'. Explain that a document has a hierarchy—chapters, sections, paragraphs. Instead of cutting blindly, we should cut at natural 'seams'. Use the example of a technical manual: a chunk should ideally contain a complete instruction rather than half an instruction and half a table of contents. Explain that the goal is 'High Cohesion, Low Coupling'—each chunk should be a self-contained unit of meaning. If the learner is coming from a programming background, compare this to modular function design.

Transition to the 'Embedding' process, which transforms these text chunks into mathematical coordinates. Draw a 2D or 3D coordinate system. Explain that an embedding model takes a chunk of text and assigns it a location in a high-dimensional space (e.g., 1536 dimensions for OpenAI's models). The core intuition here is that 'distance equals difference'. Words or chunks about 'dogs' will be physically close to 'puppies' but far from 'quantum physics'. This is why preprocessing is so critical: if our chunks are messy or nonsensical, their position in this space will be 'noisy,' and the retrieval system will fail to find them later.

Conduct a thought exercise regarding the trade-offs of chunk size. Ask the learner to imagine a 50-page PDF. If chunks are too small (e.g., 50 tokens), we lose the broader narrative. If they are too large (e.g., 2000 tokens), the 'signal-to-noise' ratio drops because the chunk contains too much irrelevant information around the specific fact we need. Explain that finding the 'Goldilocks zone' is an empirical process, often requiring testing multiple sizes to see which yields the most accurate retrieval. This prepares the learner for the reality that RAG is as much about data engineering as it is about AI.

tasks: Calculate the trade-off between small and large chunk sizes for a 50-page PDF document.
Compare different chunking strategies (character-based vs. semantic-based) for a technical manual.

sessions.title: Vector Stores and Search
sessions.description: This session introduces vector databases and the algorithms used to perform similarity search, such as Cosine Similarity. You will understand how to store embeddings and retrieve the most relevant pieces of information in milliseconds. This enables you to scale your AI applications to handle millions of documents without losing speed or accuracy.
sessions.sessionOutline:
Start the session by addressing the transition from raw embeddings to a searchable library. While we know embeddings represent meaning as coordinates in space, we must now solve the 'needle in a haystack' problem: if we have a million document chunks, how do we find the top three most relevant ones in milliseconds? This session moves from the mathematical definition of 'similarity' to the architectural reality of a Vector Store. Begin on the whiteboard by drawing a 2D coordinate system. Place a 'Query' vector and several 'Document' vectors. This visualization is crucial to help students move past thinking of databases as keyword-matchers and start seeing them as spatial retrieval systems.

Introduce Cosine Similarity as our primary metric for relevance. Explain that in high-dimensional AI space, the 'length' of a vector (how much text was in the chunk) is often less important than the 'direction' it points (the semantic meaning). On the whiteboard, derive the formula: the dot product divided by the product of the magnitudes. Walk through a manual calculation using two-dimensional vectors like [1, 0] and [0, 1] to show that perpendicular vectors have zero similarity, while [1, 1] and [2, 2] have a similarity of 1 despite different lengths. This clarifies why a short query can match a long document chunk if the underlying 'topic' or vector direction aligns.

Address the 'Scalability Trap'—the common misconception that we can simply calculate similarity against every document for every query. Explain that as the dataset grows to millions of vectors, a 'Brute Force' or 'Flat Search' becomes a bottleneck that kills application performance. Use this to introduce the concept of Vector Indexing. Compare it to a library's Dewey Decimal System; we need a way to narrow down the search area before we start doing the heavy math. Illustrate the concept of HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small Worlds) or IVF (Inverted File Index) by drawing clusters on the board, showing how we first find the 'neighborhood' of the query before looking for the exact neighbors. This transition from 'Exact Search' to 'Approximate Nearest Neighbor' (ANN) search is the most important leap for a production engineer.

Transition to the role of a Vector Database as more than just a search engine. A true Vector Store handles CRUD operations, metadata filtering, and persistence. Explain the 'Metadata Filtering' challenge: how do we find vectors that are semantically similar *and* were created after 2023? Explain the two approaches—pre-filtering and post-filtering—and the potential pitfalls of each, such as the 'empty result' problem if the filter is too restrictive. This part of the lecture ensures that students don't just see this as a math problem, but as a database management task.

Conclude by setting up the practice tasks. Have the students perform a manual cosine similarity check to solidify the 'direction over magnitude' concept. Then, challenge them to choose an indexing strategy for a hypothetical high-traffic app. This exercise reveals whether they understand the trade-off between search speed (latency), memory usage, and accuracy (recall). Remind them that in RAG, a slightly less 'accurate' vector search that returns results in 10ms is often better than a perfect search that takes 2 seconds.

tasks: Perform a manual cosine similarity calculation between three simplified vector representations.
Select an appropriate indexing strategy for a high-traffic vector search application.

sessions.title: Designing a RAG System That Works
sessions.description: This session synthesizes the previous concepts into a complete pipeline, addressing common failure modes like 'lost in the middle' or irrelevant retrieval. You will learn how to rank results and format the retrieved context into the final prompt. This session directly empowers you to build the core engine of modern LLM-based enterprise search tools.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by transitioning from the 'parts' of RAG to the 'whole.' The central thesis of this session is that a RAG system is only as strong as its weakest link: even perfect retrieval is useless if the generation phase ignores the context or becomes overwhelmed by it. Start the whiteboard by drawing a unified pipeline that connects the vector store from the previous session to the final LLM response. Introduce the concept of the 'Context Window bottleneck.' The teacher should explain that while LLMs have large windows, they suffer from a 'U-shaped' performance curve, often referred to as 'lost in the middle.' Illustrate this on the board with a graph showing that models effectively recall information at the very beginning and end of a provided context but struggle with the middle sections. This motivates the need for ranking and careful prompt construction.

Moving into the architectural design of the prompt, the teacher should demonstrate how to structure the 'System Prompt' versus the 'User Context.' Use the whiteboard to layout a template that clearly separates instructions, retrieved documents, and the user's question using delimiters like XML tags or triple backticks. The key takeaway here is 'role clarity.' If the model cannot distinguish between its internal knowledge and the 'provided context,' it will revert to hallucinations. Highlight a common mistake: developers often just concatenate text. Instead, show how to inject instructions like 'If the answer is not in the provided documents, state that you do not know'—this is a critical safety guardrail that turns a generic LLM into a specialized knowledge assistant.

Next, introduce the 'Re-ranking' stage as a bridge between retrieval and generation. Explain that vector search (semantic similarity) is fast but sometimes 'blunt.' A re-ranker acts as a second, more expensive filter that evaluates the top-K results for actual relevance to the question. On the board, show a scenario where a user asks about 'Apple the company' but the vector search returns 'Apple the fruit' because of high similarity in a narrow context. The re-ranker is the logic gate that fixes this. This teaches students that the quality of the 'Context' is a curated selection process, not just a raw data dump.

We then address the 'Citing Sources' requirement, which is vital for enterprise trust. The teacher should walk through how to instruct the model to use citations like [Document 1] or [Ref 2]. This isn't just for the user's benefit; it forces the model to attend to specific parts of the retrieved text during the token generation process. Use an exercise here: ask students to identify a failure where a model provides a correct answer but cites the wrong document. This reveals a 'hallucination of reference,' a subtle but dangerous error type. Explain that this usually happens because the prompt didn't explicitly link document IDs to the content chunks.

Finally, the session concludes with a diagnostic framework for 'Debugging the RAG Loop.' The teacher should draw a flowchart for troubleshooting: if the answer is wrong, is it because the retriever didn't find the document (Retrieval Failure), or because the LLM ignored the document (Generation Failure)? This distinction is the most important skill for a production engineer. By looking at the 'Top-K' results vs. the final output, students learn to isolate whether they need to fix their chunking/indexing or their prompt engineering. End with the principle that a RAG system is a living feedback loop, not a static script.

tasks: Design a prompt template that effectively incorporates retrieved context while instructing the model to cite its sources.
Analyze a RAG system failure and identify if the error occurred during retrieval or generation.

lectures.title: Tools and Agents
lectures.description: This lecture explores the frontier of LLM autonomy, where models move beyond text to perform actions in the real world through tool use and recursive planning.

sessions.title: Function Calling
sessions.description: This session teaches you how models are trained to output structured arguments for specific functions instead of conversational text. You will learn how to define tool schemas that an LLM can understand and 'call' when appropriate. This is the primary bridge between the probabilistic world of AI and the deterministic world of APIs and databases.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by addressing the fundamental friction between how Large Language Models naturally communicate—through probabilistic text generation—and how our software systems operate—through deterministic, structured data. This session introduces 'Function Calling' not just as a feature, but as a paradigm shift where the model stops trying to 'answer' the user and instead prepares an instruction for a machine. Start by visualizing a bridge on the whiteboard: on one side is the 'Fuzzy World' of tokens and human language, and on the other is the 'Rigid World' of APIs, SQL, and Python functions. The core idea is that we aren't asking the AI to do the math or check the weather; we are asking it to pick the right tool and fill out the order form correctly.

To move from intuition to technical implementation, we introduce the concept of the JSON Schema. This is the 'User Manual' we provide to the LLM. On the whiteboard, map out a standard function definition, highlighting the 'name', 'description', and 'parameters' fields. The most important lesson here is that the LLM is not actually 'executing' the function—it is merely predicting the most likely string of text that matches a specific schema. A common pitfall is the belief that the model knows what a function does by magic; emphasize that the quality of the 'description' field is the most critical factor for model performance. If the description is vague, the model will hallucinate arguments or fail to trigger the tool when needed.

Next, we walk through the 'Tool Call Loop,' a three-step cycle that often confuses newcomers. Step one: the user asks a question. Step two: the model identifies a tool match and outputs a specifically formatted JSON string (the 'call'). Step three: the system (not the model) executes the code and feeds the result back to the model as a 'tool' role message. It is vital to show that the model doesn't see the real-time execution; it only sees the result after the fact. Visualizing this back-and-forth flow on the board helps students understand that the LLM is the 'brain' while the application code is the 'hands.' This distinction is what prevents developers from expecting the LLM to magically have access to a database without a middleware connector.

We conclude with a practice moment where students draft a JSON schema for a weather API. The goal here is to expose how specific we must be—for example, does the model know if the temperature should be in Celsius or Fahrenheit? By forcing the students to define an 'enum' for units, they realize that they must constrain the model's creative freedom to ensure system stability. This session sets the stage for the entire unit: once you can force a model to speak in JSON, you can integrate it into any software stack in the world.

tasks: Write a JSON schema for a 'get_weather' tool and verify if a model correctly populates the arguments.
Trace the loop of a model requesting a tool call, the execution of that call, and the model's final response.

sessions.title: Tool Use Patterns
sessions.description: This session examines how models choose between multiple available tools to solve a complex request. You will learn about routing logic and how to handle scenarios where the model needs to use tools sequentially. Mastering these patterns allows you to build assistants that can interact with calendars, emails, and databases seamlessly.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by transitioning from the 'what' of function calling—the syntax and structured output—to the 'how' of complex orchestration. The primary objective today is to help students understand that an LLM is not just a translator for JSON, but a router. I will start the whiteboard by drawing a central model hub surrounded by disparate external systems like a CRM, a calendar API, and a search engine. The key idea here is 'Tool Selection Logic.' I’ll explain that when a user asks to 'check my schedule and email a summary to Sarah,' the model isn't just executing a command; it's performing a cognitive triage, determining which tools are relevant and in what specific order they must be invoked.

I will then introduce the concept of 'Routing Ambiguity' using a live whiteboard diagram. I’ll draw two similar tool boxes: 'Internal_Wiki_Search' and 'Public_Google_Search.' The core friction we must address is how a model decides between them. If the descriptions are vague, the model will hallucinate a guess. I’ll demonstrate how to write 'discriminative tool descriptions'—instead of just naming a tool 'Search,' we must explicitly state 'Use this ONLY for private company policy' versus 'Use this for general world facts.' This highlights that the developer’s role has shifted from writing logic gates to writing semantically clear documentation that the LLM 'reads' to make decisions.

Moving into 'Sequential Orchestration,' I will visualize a multi-step dependency chain. We’ll map out a scenario where Tool A's output (e.g., a flight confirmation number) is required as an input for Tool B (e.g., a hotel booking). I’ll draw this as a recursive loop on the board: User Prompt -> LLM -> Tool A -> Observation -> LLM -> Tool B. A common pitfall here is 'Input Drift,' where the model forgets the original user intent because it gets too focused on the intermediate technical data from the first tool. I’ll teach the students to maintain a 'scratchpad' or system prompt that reminds the model of the ultimate goal throughout the sequence.

For the practice phase, I’ll challenge the students to design a multi-tool environment for a personal assistant. Instead of just listing tools, they must define the 'Conflict Resolution' strategy: what happens if the Search tool says it's raining but the Calendar tool says 'Outdoor Picnic'? This exercise is designed to reveal if students understand that tools can provide contradictory data and that the LLM must be coached on which source is the 'source of truth.' We will conclude by refining tool schemas to ensure that similar API endpoints (like 'get_user_by_id' vs 'get_user_by_email') have distinct enough descriptions to prevent the model from mixing up argument types.

tasks: Design a multi-tool environment for a personal assistant bot (e.g., Search + Calculator + Email).
Optimize tool descriptions to prevent the model from confusing two similar API endpoints.

sessions.title: Agent Loops and Planning
sessions.description: This session explores autonomous frameworks like ReAct (Reason + Act), where the model iteratively plans and executes actions. You will learn how to maintain state across multiple turns of logic to solve open-ended goals. This session is the pinnacle of the unit, moving you from static prompt-response cycles to dynamic, goal-oriented systems.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin by pivoting from the 'stateless' nature of simple function calling to the 'stateful' concept of an autonomous agent. The central theme of this session is bridging the gap between a model that merely answers and a model that thinks and acts. I will start by drawing a simple loop on the whiteboard: Observation -> Thought -> Action. I want to emphasize that while a basic LLM is a text predictor, an agent is a system where the model’s prediction becomes a driver for external operations. This transition is the 'pinnacle' of Unit 4 because it demonstrates how we can overcome the context window's linear nature by allowing the model to recursively update its own plan.

The core of our technical discussion centers on the ReAct (Reason + Act) framework. On the whiteboard, I will deconstruct a complex query, such as 'Compare the stock price of Apple with the current inflation rate and write a summary.' Instead of the model trying to guess the answer in one go, I’ll show how the model generates a 'Thought' block—a hidden internal monologue where it admits what it doesn't know. Then, I’ll draw the 'Action' block where it selects a tool. The key insight here for the students is that the 'Thought' acts as a cognitive buffer, preventing the model from hallucinating a direct answer by forcing it to articulate a plan first. I will warn them that skipping the 'Reason' step often leads to the model picking the wrong tool or parameters.

Next, we will look at the 'Loop' itself. I’ll visualize the system prompt as a perpetual cycle: the model receives an observation (the tool output), appends it to its memory, and then generates the next 'Thought.' This is where I introduce the challenge of state management. We need to discuss how the LLM 'remembers' what it has already tried. A common pitfall for developers is failing to truncate or summarize this loop history, leading to 'Context Exhaustion' where the model forgets the original goal because the tool outputs were too verbose. I will suggest a 'Reflective' step in the loop where the model periodically summarizes its progress toward the goal to keep the context clean.

To solidify these concepts, we will walk through a 'Trace Analysis' exercise. I’ll present a log of a failing agent that is stuck in a loop—perhaps it keeps searching for the same term but getting no results. We will discuss how to implement 'Retry Logic' and 'Self-Correction.' Instead of the system crashing on a 404 error, the script should show how a well-prompted agent can 'Reason' that the URL was wrong and try an alternative. This teaches the students that agency is not just about success, but about the robust handling of deterministic failures in the environment.

Finally, we will conclude by designing a basic error-recovery loop. I will draw a flow chart where a tool error is fed back into the 'Observation' slot. This is a critical mental shift: the error is not a bug in the code, but a new piece of data for the model to process. We’ll discuss why setting a 'max_iterations' limit is a non-negotiable safety feature, preventing the agent from spending infinite API credits on a logic loop it cannot solve. By the end of the session, the learners should see the LLM not as a calculator, but as a fallible yet adaptable 'manager' of a complex workflow.

tasks: Deconstruct a ReAct trace to identify where the model 'reasoned' and where it 'acted'.
Design a simple loop that allows a model to retry a task if the first tool execution returns an error.

sessions.title: Agent Failure Modes
sessions.description: This session identifies why agents fail, focusing on infinite loops, hallucinated tool arguments, and context window exhaustion. You will learn defensive programming techniques to make your agentic systems more robust for production. Understanding these risks is critical for building safe and reliable autonomous agents that don't spin out of control.
sessions.sessionOutline:
We begin this session by pivoting from the excitement of autonomous agency to the sobering reality of production: agents are fragile. The core concept to introduce here is the 'Probability of Failure Accumulation.' In a standard LLM call, you have one chance for a hallucination; in an agent loop, every 'Thought,' 'Action,' and 'Observation' cycle acts as a multiplier for potential error. We will draw a flowchart on the whiteboard showing a simple loop, then start marking 'X's where things go wrong: the LLM might hallucinate a tool that doesn't exist, provide arguments in the wrong format (JSON syntax errors), or misunderstand a tool's error message as a successful result.

The first major failure mode to visualize is the 'Infinite Loop' or 'Circular Reasoning.' This happens when the LLM gets stuck in a state where it believes it needs more information but keeps calling the same ineffective tool, or when it keeps repeating the same thought process without taking a new action. On the whiteboard, we'll illustrate this as a 'Drain'—where the context window fills up with repetitive logs, leading to 'Context Exhaustion.' I will explain that as the context grows, the model's 'attention' becomes diluted, making it even more likely to make mistakes, creating a death spiral of cost and latency. This is why we must introduce the 'Hard Ceiling' concept—a mandatory 'max_iterations' guardrail that kills the process regardless of whether the goal is met.

Next, we shift to 'Tool Execution Failures,' specifically focusing on how the LLM handles deterministic chaos like a 500 Server Error or a Timeout. Most beginners assume the model will intuitively know what a '404 Not Found' means, but without explicit instruction, the model might hallucinate that the data was 'hidden' or 'deleted' rather than recognizing a network issue. We'll use the whiteboard to draft a 'Defensive Prompting' layer. This involves teaching the model that an error message from a tool is a valid observation to be reasoned about, not a personal failure. We'll walk through a pseudo-code implementation of an 'Error Handler' that translates cryptic stack traces into human-readable (and LLM-readable) instructions, such as 'The search service is down; please try the database tool instead.'

Finally, we will address 'State Drift'—the phenomenon where the agent forgets its original objective because the tool outputs are too long or distracting. To fix this, we'll discuss the 'System Anchor' technique, where the original goal is re-injected into every turn of the loop. For the practice segment, I'll have the students intentionally break their agents by giving them a broken tool. This is designed to reveal a common misconception: that the LLM is 'smart' enough to fix code on the fly. By watching the agent fail to handle a 500 error, students learn that the 'intelligence' of an agent is only as good as the error-handling logic and guardrails designed by the engineer.

tasks: Implement a 'max_iterations' guardrail to prevent an agent from looping infinitely.
Test an agent's response to a tool returning a 500 error and implement a recovery strategy.
